records.citation: Ahamed, A., Knight, R., Alam, S., Pauloo, R., & Melton, F. (2021). Assessing the utility of remote sensing data to accurately estimate changes in groundwater storage. Science of the Total Environment, 807, 150635. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.150635
records.geography: California's Central Valley, basin-wide, 2002-2020
records.analysis_method: Estimates groundwater storage change using an ensemble remote-sensing water balance (precipitation, ET, soil moisture, runoff, reservoir storage); validates against three independent methods: GRACE satellite data, groundwater wells, and a groundwater flow model
records.accounting_method: Remote sensing water balance (ensemble of satellite/reanalysis products); GRACE gravimetry; well-based measurement; numerical groundwater flow model
records.key_finding:
- Remote sensing storage estimates are reasonably reliable at basin scale, within 15% of wells/models
- ET remains the weak link in the water balance chain; precipitation is the strongest input
- RS offers a genuine advantage in latency - sub-annual vs. the multi-year lag typical of wells/models
- Method-validation study; no GSA-level implementation described
records.comparative_finding: Remote-sensing-based estimates correlated well with independent methods; annual trends during droughts fell within 15% of well- and model-based trends; ET identified as the highest-uncertainty water balance component, precipitation the lowest; RS uniquely enables sub-annual latency not achievable with wells or models
records.study_context: Basin-wide Central Valley scale; method explicitly noted as best suited to regions where net groundwater in/outflow is small relative to other water balance components

records.citation: Anderson, M., Gao, F., Knipper, K., Hain, C., Dulaney, W., Baldocchi, D., et al. (2018). Field-scale assessment of land and water use change over the California delta using remote sensing. Remote Sensing, 10(6), 889. https://doi.org/10.3390/rs10060889
records.geography: California Delta, water years 2015-2016
records.analysis_method: Multi-sensor thermal remote sensing (Landsat + MODIS data fusion) to map field-scale, daily-timestep evapotranspiration; validated against 8 eddy-covariance flux towers spanning different crops and a chronosequence of restored wetlands; produces a 2-year, 30-m ET datacube combined with annual land-use classification
records.accounting_method: Thermal remote sensing ET (multi-sensor data fusion); eddy-covariance ground-truth measurement; conventional water-balance/crop-coefficient ET (contrasted against as the prior standard)
records.data_sources: GOES East/West geostationary thermal imagery (ALEXI baseline); Landsat 7 and 8 thermal bands (sharpened 30m, Data Mining Sharpener); MODIS Terra MOD11_L2 swath LST (1km); MODIS MCD15A3 LAI product (downscaled to 30m); CFSR meteorological reanalysis (0.25° resolution); LandIQ land use classifications 2015-2016 (30m, 36 classes); eight AmeriFlux/GRAPEX eddy covariance towers; STARFM spatial-temporal fusion algorithm.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program. Study commissioned in part by the State Water Resources Control Board Delta Watermaster Office as part of an ET model intercomparison study to evaluate capabilities for water accounting in support of SGMA. Authors explicitly frame the land use conversion water use matrix as a tool for policymakers to assess water use change scenarios in response to incentives such as carbon or conservation credits.
records.key_finding:
- Diagnostic remote-sensing ET explicitly contrasted against conventional water-balance/crop-coefficient methods
- Accuracy improves substantially at longer timesteps (daily RMSE 0.95 to annual RMSE 0.28 mm/day)
- Captures real-world land-use change impacts (crop conversion) on water use, not just idealized estimates
- Framed as statewide-scalable; no GSA-level implementation described
records.direct_quotes:
"This study describes an approach for operational accounting of water usage by landcover type and water management strategy, with a geographic focus on the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta region of California." (Introduction, p. 3)

"The water accounting information in Figures 14–17 can be used to assess specific scenarios of water use change in response to incentives (e.g., carbon or conservation credits) and stressors (e.g., restrictions in water allocations in times of drought). For example, if the carbon market became more viable and farmers were incentivized to transition a percentage of fallowed or pasture land to wetlands, the resulting change in regional water demands could be predicted." (Results, Section 3.2, p. 21)
records.accounting_gap: Water use change estimates are specific to the drought conditions of 2015-2016 — climate contributions from interannual variability are not separated from land use change effects, creating an additionality problem for crediting. Classification errors between similar crop types (alfalfa vs. other deciduous) produced implausible ET differences, indicating land use classification accuracy is as important as ET model accuracy for reliable water savings accounting. Restored wetland ET decreases over time as vegetation matures — early-stage water savings from converting irrigated agriculture to wetland may not persist in the long term.
records.comparative_finding: RMSE of 0.95, 0.76, 0.58, and 0.28 mm/day at daily, weekly, monthly, and annual timesteps respectively; argues diagnostic remote-sensing ET reflects real-world conditions (poor/variable stands, sub-optimal irrigation) that idealized water-balance/crop-coefficient techniques miss
records.study_context: Drought-stressed Delta following a multi-year drought; corn and alfalfa identified as highest water users, with a notable ET decrease from 2015 to 2016 due to conversion to less water-intensive crops
records.notes:
Operationalizes water accounting by landcover type and managemnet strategy, but are specific to 2015-2016 drought conditions.

36 different land use-conversion pairs were asssessed created by combing ALEXI energy balance modeling with LandIQ LULC. (pre-OpenET days)

Restored wetlands have very high ET (similar to irrigated crops) at the onset, but ET declines over time and water savings are more apparent in the long-term.

records.citation: Bachand, P.A.M., Roy, S.B., Choperena, J., Cameron, D., & Horwath, W.R. (2014). Implications of using on-farm flood flow capture to recharge groundwater and mitigate flood risks along the Kings River, CA. Environmental Science & Technology, 48(23), 13601-13609.
records.geography: Terranova Ranch, western Fresno County, California, USA (~1,000 acres; adjacent to James Bypass on Kings River); San Joaquin Valley alluvial soils (Fresno sandy loam series with cemented duripan); January to July 2011 flood season
records.accounting_method: (1) Check-level infiltration accounting: 11 study checks (field subdivisions separated by berms) each equipped with pressure transducers and staff gauges measuring standing water depth at 15-min intervals; inflows and outflows ceased after flooding began; infiltration + ET = rate of water level decline; direct recharge rate = infiltration rate - ET, where ET calculated from CIMIS Westlands Station #105 reference ET × crop coefficient. (2) Vadose zone water front tracking: Decagon ECH2O TE soil probes (N=3 per check) at 15cm, 60cm, and 120cm depth monitoring volumetric water content and EC at 15-min intervals; depth of applied water front estimated from minimum/maximum soil water capacity of site-specific soil cores. (3) Farm-scale water budget: Teledyne ISCO Acoustic Velocity Meter recording KR inflows to Terranova Canal at 15-min intervals; irrigator records of pump start/stop times and water allocation per field; CIMIS precipitation and ET data combined to calculate check-level and farm-scale water budgets; direct recharge versus in-lieu recharge partitioned from farm records.
records.data_sources: Pressure transducers and staff gauges in 11 study checks (15-min interval); Teledyne ISCO Acoustic Velocity Meter at Kings River diversion (15-min interval); Decagon ECH2O TE soil moisture probes (15-min, three depths); CIMIS Westlands Station #105; Geoprobe soil cores to 3m (EC and gravimetric moisture); YSI datasonde (EC and temperature at check locations and groundwater well); UC Davis Soil Biology and Biochemistry lab (water quality); NRCS Web Soil Survey; STATISTICA statistical software.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program. Study funded by NRCS CIG grant with Sustainable Conservation as partner and Kings River Conservation District as stakeholder. Authors explicitly frame On-Farm Flood Capture and Recharge (OFFCR) as 'a new paradigm for the farming community' and conduct a 25-year cost analysis showing $36/acre-foot cost versus $95/acre-foot groundwater pumping — positioning the work as a feasibility study for future program development. A first-phase project diverting 150 cfs is noted as under construction at time of publication.
records.key_finding: Field-scale infiltration rates averaged 4.2 inches per day on Kings River alluvial soils following deep ripping of the cemented duripan layer, with 85% of captured flood flows going to in-lieu recharge and only 15% to direct recharge — meaning the dominant accounting benefit of on-farm flood flow capture in California's San Joaquin Valley is avoided groundwater pumping rather than direct aquifer storage augmentation.
records.direct_quotes:
"Direct recharge rates were calculated from infiltration rates after accounting for ET losses using reference ET and crop coefficients." (Methods, p. 13603)

"About 15% of the applied water went to direct recharge and 85% went to in lieu recharge... For the infiltration rates typical of TR (2.6-5.7 in d-1), 1 cfs captured requires 4-10 acres." (Results, p. 13604-13605)
records.accounting_gap: Study measures infiltration rate and vadose zone water movement but does not track water to the saturated zone — the same infiltration-versus-recharge gap identified in Racz et al. (2011). Infiltration rate declines over time as flooding continues, but the functional relationship between flooding duration and declining infiltration is site-specific and not generalizable without additional field data. Water quality initially deteriorates as salts and nitrates are flushed from the vadose zone into groundwater before improving — the timing and magnitude of this short-term quality impact is unquantified at aquifer scale.
records.notes:
Only CA paper in the cluster, study conducted on Terranova Ranch in west Fresno county. Could be used as a template for robust flood-MAR tracking, although requires significant investment.

Three measurement approaches used:
- pressure transducers + staff gauges measured infiltration rates
- soil moisture probes at varying depths verified water made it into the aquifer
- farm-scale water budget quantified 15/85 split of direct recharge/in-lieu recharge (result of farm operations)

records.citation: Barlow, P.M., & Leake, S.A. (2012). Streamflow depletion by wells — Understanding and managing the effects of groundwater pumping on streamflow. U.S. Geological Survey Circular 1376, 84 p.
records.geography: Western United States (broadly applicable); case studies from San Pedro Basin (Arizona), Republican River Basin (Nebraska/Kansas/Colorado), and hypothetical river-valley aquifer (northeastern US)
records.accounting_method:
(1) Conceptual framework for depletion: pumped groundwater initially comes from aquifer storage; as pumping continues, groundwater discharge to connected streams is captured (reduced baseflow) or flow is induced from stream to aquifer (losing stream); streamflow depletion = pumping rate × depletion fraction.
(2) Analytical solution (Glover-Balmer, 1954): depletion estimated as function of time, pumping rate, aquifer transmissivity and storativity, and distance from well to stream. Streambed conductance added by Hunt (1999) as a fourth parameter for low-permeability streambeds.
(3) Field measurement techniques: direct streamflow measurement at upstream and downstream gages (gain-loss survey) to detect reach-scale depletion; point streambed flux measurements using seepage meters to estimate exchange across the streambed; piezometer networks to map hydraulic head gradients at stream-aquifer interface.
(4) Response functions / SDF: Streamflow Depletion Factor (Jenkins, 1968) derived from Glover-Balmer — time for depletion rate to equal 28% of pumping rate; mappable by distance to stream, transmissivity, and storativity to support regulatory screening.
records.data_sources: USGS Groundwater Resources Program literature synthesis; MODFLOW numerical simulations (Barlow 1997) for hypothetical river-valley aquifer case; San Pedro River Basin USGS groundwater model; Republican River Compact Arbitration records; published analytical model comparisons. No new primary field datasets, strictly a synthesis and review document.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program described. Documents the regulatory use of SDF-based analytical models in Colorado and other prior appropriation states for quantifying depletion by wells near streams with senior water rights holders. Documents the Republican River Compact accounting framework (Nebraska-Kansas-Colorado) as a multi-state operational example of streamflow depletion accounting using numerical modeling for interstate water compact compliance.
records.key_finding: Field measurement of streamflow depletion is only feasible at the reach scale under controlled conditions where pumping effects can be distinguished from other stresses. Regional-scale depletion must be estimated by analytical or numerical models. Even reach-scale measurement requires careful design because non-pumping changes in streamflow can equal or exceed pumping-induced changes.
records.direct_quotes:
"Groundwater discharge is a significant component of streamflow, with groundwater contributing as much as 90 percent of annual streamflow volume in some parts of the country." (Foreword, p. iii)

"Because well A is closest to the stream, the drawdowns created at the well are larger [and] streambed seepage rates greater than zero indicate groundwater discharge to the stream and gaining streamflow conditions, whereas seepage rates less than zero indicate induced infiltration of streamflow into the aquifer and losing streamflow conditions... changes in streambed seepage rates are not confined to the reach of the stream that is immediately opposite to the wells, but instead extend both upgradient to and downgradient from the wells." (Results/Discussion, p. 23)
records.accounting_gap: Streambed conductance (resistance to flow across the streambed) is one of the most important parameters in analytical depletion models but is extremely difficult to measure at regional scale and is rarely available. Long response times between pumping initiation and measurable streamflow effects (months to decades depending on aquifer properties and well-stream distance) create fundamental challenges for monitoring and adaptive management. Attribution of observed streamflow trends to groundwater pumping versus climate variability or surface water operations is rarely achievable with field data alone.
records.notes:
Foundational USGS reference: cited by virtually every subsequent ISW accounting paper including Zipper et al. (2022).

The Foreword quote (groundwater contributing up to 90% of annual streamflow in some regions) is the most frequently cited statistic on GW-SW connectivity in SGMA contexts.

SDF appendix (Appendix C) and field techniques chapter are the most operationally useful sections for GAP ISW module design.

records.citation: Bernat, R.F.A., Megdal, S.B., & Eden, S. (2019). Long-term storage credits: Analyzing market-based transactions to achieve Arizona water policy objectives. Water, 12(2), 568.
records.geography: Arizona Active Management Areas: Phoenix, Tucson, and Pinal — covering the majority of Arizona's population; 23-year transaction record (1994-2017)
records.accounting_method:
(1) LTSC issuance accounting: ADWR tracks every cubic meter stored at each permitted USF or GSF pursuant to a water storage permit; 95% of CAP water deemed recoverable by ADWR is recorded as LTSCs, with 5% cut remaining permanently in aquifer; effluent stored at managed USF on or after 31 January 2019 subject to same 5% cut; LTSCs are static once issued — balance does not change unless water is physically recovered or extinguished for compliance.
(2) LTSC transaction analysis: 23 years of ADWR public records (1994-2017) analyzed for buyer/seller entity type, volume transacted, transaction frequency, and geographic AMA of transaction; entity categories coded as municipal water providers, investment firms, governmental entities (AWBA, CAGRD, CAWCD), agricultural sector, and individuals.
(3) Replenishment mechanism: excess groundwater pumped above AWS allocation must be replenished by storing equal volume of renewable water in the aquifer OR by extinguishing equal volume of LTSCs from a replenishment district account — LTSCs function as compliance currency.
records.data_sources: ADWR Underground Storage and Recovery Program transaction database (public records, 1994-2017); ADWR AMA annual reports for water demand by sector; AWBA annual reports for storage volumes and firming targets; CAGRD member records; Arizona water law statutes (A.R.S. §45-801 et seq.).
records.formal_program_or_crediting: Fully operational formal crediting and trading program. ADWR maintains a central accounting database tracking every LTSC issued, transferred, and extinguished since 1994. LTSCs are freely transferable by simple credit account transfer requiring no regulatory approval beyond ADWR notification. Analysis shows approximately 20 transactions per year on average, with municipal water providers and investment firms as primary buyers and AWBA and CAGRD as primary volume transactors. Market described as thin but functional.
records.key_finding: 23 years of LTSC transaction records show that recharge credits function as a viable compliance currency. Water providers use them to meet excess groundwater replenishment obligations and governmental entities use them to firm municipal water supplies against Colorado River shortages. But the market is thin, prices are not publicly disclosed, and most transactions involve governmental entities rather than private market participants.
records.direct_quotes:
"ADWR keeps track of every cubic meter of water stored at a permitted recharge facility pursuant to a water storage permit, which assures that credits are granted only for water reaching the aquifer and that the credit owner has the right to recover, sell, or extinguish the credit." (Methods, Section 2.3, p. 6)

"LTSCs have emerged as a tool for water users to achieve compliance with groundwater regulations in the most populated areas of the state, such as the cities of Phoenix and Tucson." (Abstract, p. 1)
records.accounting_gap: Buyers and sellers are not required to disclose transaction prices, making LTSC market efficiency impossible to evaluate and creating barriers for new market entrants who lack price reference points. The market is concentrated among a small number of governmental entities, meaning it functions more as a regulatory compliance mechanism than a true water market. The spatial mismatch between where water is recharged and where LTSCs are extinguished for compliance means the local hydrogeological benefits of recharge are not captured in the accounting.
records.notes:
Best available documentation of how recharge credits function in practice.

The LTSC model is the most developed western US analog for what SGMA-aligned recharge crediting could look like in California.

Limited market finding: ~20 transactions per year even after 23 years

records.citation: Bostic, D., Mendez-Barrientos, L., Pauloo, R., Dobbin, K., & MacClements, V. (2023). Thousands of domestic and public supply wells face failure despite groundwater sustainability reform in California's Central Valley. Scientific Reports, 13, 14797. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-023-41379-9
records.geography: California, Central Valley (35 groundwater subbasins)
records.analysis_method: The study models projected groundwater levels under the minimum thresholds that local Groundwater Sustainability Agencies set as their own definition of sustainability in their Groundwater Sustainability Plans, then compares those thresholds against well construction records to estimate how many domestic and public supply wells would fail (fully or partially dewatered) if the locally-set thresholds are actually reached; well failure risk is then cross-referenced against Disadvantaged Community (DAC) boundaries and each subbasin's groundwater monitoring network coverage.
records.key_finding: Locally-set sustainability thresholds are, in most subbasins, consistent with continued business-as-usual groundwater decline rather than genuinely protective, and if reached could dewater over 9,000 domestic wells and roughly 1,000 public supply wells across the Central Valley; Disadvantaged Communities face well failure at about the same rate as everyone else, but with fewer financial resources to recover.
records.direct_quotes: "We find that 55% of DACs (n=106) within groundwater basin boundaries are fully represented in monitoring networks (>90% of area covered)... However, 31 DACs in 11 [Groundwater Sustainability Plans] have at least 50% of their area outside of [plan] monitoring networks. Finally, nearly 15% of domestic and public supply wells that fall within DAC boundaries (n=508) are entirely outside of monitoring networks." (Results)
records.learnings: Nearly 15% of domestic and public supply wells inside Disadvantaged Community boundaries sit entirely outside their local groundwater monitoring network, and 31 Disadvantaged Communities have at least half their area unmonitored — meaning some of the highest-risk communities are also the ones with the least existing groundwater data to work with, a mapped and quantified gap rather than an assumed one.
records.community_selection: Not applicable — this is a quantitative geospatial/hydrologic modeling study using well-construction records, published Groundwater Sustainability Plan thresholds, and DAC boundary data; there is no primary interview, survey, or engagement process.
records.notes: Not an engagement-process paper — a quantitative outcomes/monitoring-coverage study, so its relevance to Community Considerations is substantive equity in monitoring infrastructure, not participation process. The monitoring-coverage gap finding is a concrete, mappable complement to Cantor (2021)'s decision-data gap-analysis method — together they suggest GAP could run a similar audit checking whether its own groundwater monitoring inputs have equivalent blind spots in DAC areas. Co-authored by Dobbin; cross-reference with her other three papers already in this sheet.
records.engagement_type_raw: Community Equity (primary); Data Transparency (secondary — monitoring network coverage gap finding)

records.citation: Cantor, A., Kiparsky, M., Hubbard, S. S., Kennedy, R., Pecharroman, L. C., Guivetchi, K., Darling, G., McCready, C., & Bales, R. (2021). Making a Water Data System Responsive to Information Needs of Decision Makers. Frontiers in Climate, 3, 761444. DOI: 10.3389/fclim.2021.761444
records.geography: California, statewide
records.analysis_method: Led by the California Department of Water Resources (DWR), the California Council on Science and Technology, and University of California researchers under California's Open and Transparent Water Data Act, the study developed 20 "use cases" — structured descriptions pairing a real water-management decision with the data needed to make it — through three full-day facilitated workshops plus targeted stakeholder meetings; data sources and gaps for each use case were coded and cross-checked by multiple researchers to build a typology of data limitations (availability, accessibility, interoperability, resolution).
records.key_finding: A structured, decision-first method (define the decision, then work backward to the data it requires) found that the hardest data gaps to close are the smallest share of total data sources (about 10%) but are disproportionately important to specific high-stakes decisions, including a worked example on groundwater recharge project planning under the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act.
records.direct_quotes: "Federal and state agencies made up about 90% of the data sources, and could readily adapt to a federated data system... The remaining 10% of more-specialized data, central to important decisions across multiple use cases, would require additional investment or incentives to achieve data consistency, interoperability, and compatibility." (Abstract/Results)
records.learnings: The paper explicitly cautions that meaningful stakeholder engagement is time- and resource-intensive and warns not to underestimate the facilitation capacity required; the method's real-world adoption (California's AB 1755 Partner Agency Team formally adopted its federated data system recommendation) is itself evidence the approach translates from research into practice.
records.community_selection: Workshop participants (60-80 per session for the first two workshops, ~100 at a final feedback forum) were purposively sampled to include state and local agency staff, academics, non-profit representatives, and community members with direct experience producing or using water data; four additional use cases came from targeted meetings with subject-matter experts, and eight more from direct work with non-governmental organizations and state agencies.
records.notes:
Methodologically the strongest gap-analysis precedent in the review, but its stakeholder base is water decision-makers broadly, not disadvantaged communities specifically.

Gives GAP a proven audit method, not evidence the method surfaces equity-specific data needs. The process is a bit involved but would be useful for matching community needs to data layers.

Includes a directly relevant worked example: a completed use case on groundwater recharge project planning under SGMA.

records.citation: Castaldo, G., Visser, A., Fogg, G.E., & Harter, T. (2021). Effect of groundwater age and recharge source on nitrate concentrations in domestic wells in the San Joaquin Valley. Environmental Science & Technology, 55(4), 2265–2275.
records.geography: San Joaquin Valley, California, USA (354 domestic wells sampled for water chemistry, stable isotopes, and noble gases)
records.accounting_method: (1) Groundwater age dating: apparent ³H/³He ages calculated as ln(³Hetrit/³H + 1)/0.05626 for 185 wells with analytical uncertainty <10 years; noble gas recharge temperature (NGRT) estimated from Ar and Kr concentrations using χ² minimization. (2) Recharge source classification: wells classified as 'river water recharge' using two thresholds — δ¹⁸O < -12‰ (river signature) or NGRT < 17.5°C; fraction of river water recharge (fRWR) calculated from δ¹⁸O mixing between river endmember (δ¹⁸O = -12.7‰) and local precipitation endmember (δ¹⁸O = -8.2‰). (3) Statistical analysis: Kendall-Theil-Sen-Siegel (KTSS) nonparametric regression used to quantify trends in NO₃-N with well depth proxies and groundwater age; Wilcoxon rank-sum tests used to compare NO₃-N distributions across recharge source groups and distance-to-river thresholds (1 km and 2 km).
records.data_sources: Geochemical samples from 354 domestic wells (water chemistry, δ¹⁸O, tritium, noble gases Ar/Kr/He); DWR public groundwater level data for water table depth estimation; San Joaquin Valley domestic well database; Visser et al. (2013) for noble gas methodology; SGMA Data Viewer (DWR) for basin delineations.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No operational crediting program. Authors explicitly state findings 'support the idea that flood-managed aquifer recharge may be considered for remediation of groundwater nitrate when designing replenishment of aquifers'. Framed as evidence base for MAR policy design, not a crediting mechanism.
records.key_finding: Domestic wells with river water recharge signatures (δ¹⁸O < -12‰ or NGRT < 17.5°C) have statistically significantly lower NO₃-N concentrations than wells with mixed or local precipitation recharge, and NO₃-N decreases at 0.12 mg/L per year of groundwater age — providing a geochemical basis for attributing flood-MAR water quality co-benefits to DAC domestic wells.
records.direct_quotes:
"The wells with a 'river water' signature (δ¹⁸O < −12‰) have a lower concentration of NO₃-N than other wells (Wilcoxon rank-sum test with continuity correction, p < 0.001)... wells that are further than 2 km from rivers were found to have higher NO₃-N concentration than the ones that are closer than 2 km (Wilcoxon rank-sum test with continuity correction, p < 0.05)." (Results, p. 2270)

"This study confirms that agricultural MAR ('flood-MAR') has the potential to play an important role in the remediation of groundwater quality in the SJV while also replenishing aquifers in overdraft." (Discussion, p. 2272)
records.accounting_gap: Noble gas age dating does not capture vadose zone travel time variability — a significant source of uncertainty in translating surface recharge events to domestic well nitrate outcomes. Long groundwater travel times (decades) mean nitrate benefits of MAR will not manifest in domestic wells for years to decades, creating a major temporal attribution problem for near-term crediting systems. No quantitative framework is provided for estimating the magnitude of nitrate reduction at a specific well from a specific recharge volume.
records.notes:
Most relevant to water quality co-benefit accounting rather than water quantity. The δ¹⁸O and NGRT thresholds are measurable in monitoring wells to estimate the source of groundwater (precip or river).

Long travel time lag is the challenge for incorporating this into near-term GAP crediting. But we can say: flood-MAR delivering low-nitrate Sierra Nevada river water contributes to long-term nitrate reduction in downgradient domestic wells.

No qunatification of amt of gw needed for contamination reduction.

records.citation: Corson-Dosch, N.T., Erickson, T.A., Westenbroek, S.M., Leaf, A.T., & Hunt, R.J. (2025). Estimating floodplain infiltration during overbank floods using multiple methods on a restored urban stream. Hydrological Processes, 39(1), e70054.
records.geography: Underwood Creek, Wauwatosa, Wisconsin, USA — restored urban stream reach, Menomonee River watershed; 4-year monitoring period 2018-2021; 3 floodplain monitoring clusters with groundwater wells and temperature sensors
records.accounting_method: (1) Groundwater level response: 11 shallow floodplain wells (1.2-2.6m depth) monitored at 15-min intervals; hydraulic head difference between floodplain wells and adjacent stream calculated during flood events to determine when vertical gradient was favorable for infiltration versus groundwater discharge. (2) Heat tracer: vertical temperature profiles at 10cm, 20cm, and 30cm depth in floodplain sediment monitored at 15-min intervals; VFLUX2 software applied to diurnal temperature signals to estimate vertical fluid flux using 1D heat transport equation. (3) Inundation-based storage: high-resolution lidar topography (0.5m) combined with stream stage measurements used to delineate floodplain inundation area and calculate ponded water volume at each stage; volume loss between time steps used to estimate infiltration rate when outflow pathways were constrained. (4) Vadose zone storage: unsaturated soil volume estimated from depth to water table (groundwater monitoring wells) and floodplain surface elevation (lidar); total available vadose storage calculated as physical upper bound on infiltration during each flood event.
records.data_sources: 11 shallow groundwater monitoring wells with pressure transducers (15-min interval); 3 soil temperature sensor arrays at multiple depths (15-min interval); USGS stream stage gauge; 0.5m lidar topography (Southeastern Wisconsin Regional Planning Commission); VFLUX2 software for heat tracer flux estimation; Wisconsin DNR flood event records 2018-2021.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program. Study designed as a methodology comparison to inform how floodplain infiltration can be measured and quantified for restored stream projects. Authors explicitly frame results as relevant to evaluating flood attenuation and groundwater recharge co-benefits of stream restoration.
records.key_finding: Only 0.08-0.52% of total flood volume vertically infiltrated into the floodplain aquifer across all four methods and all flood events — with hydraulic gradients favorable for infiltration occurring only at flood onset and gradients favorable for groundwater discharge to stream occurring 98% of the time — directly challenging the assumption that floodplain inundation extent can serve as a proxy for recharge volume in flood-MAR accounting.
records.direct_quotes:
"Results from all methods indicate that the volume of water that vertically infiltrates during floods is likely small relative to the total volume of the flood, with 0.08%–0.52% of flood water infiltrating into the floodplain, on average." (Abstract, p. 1)

"Gradients favourable for infiltration typically occurred during the onset of flooding but, over the study period, were mostly (98% of the time) favourable for groundwater discharge to the channel (non-flood periods). These findings highlight the importance of considering surface-groundwater dynamics, floodplain soils, and unsaturated floodplain volume in defining the benefits of floodplain infiltration for flood attenuation." (Abstract, p. 1)
records.accounting_gap: Total inundation extent and volume — the most commonly used proxy for flood recharge in water accounting — systematically overstates actual vertical infiltration because most flood water returns to the stream laterally rather than infiltrating into the aquifer. Hydraulic gradient reversal during non-flood periods means GW discharge to stream is the dominant flux, not recharge. Spatial heterogeneity in clogging layer conductance across the floodplain means point-based heat tracer measurements may not be representative of the whole floodplain.
records.notes:
Rigorous methods comparison in WI.

Volume of infiltration during floods only 0.08-0.52% of total flood so claiming recharge credits based on total inundated volume could overstate benefits by 200-1,000x.

The four-method comparison framework (groundwater levels, heat tracer, inundation storage, vadose zone storage) could be used for CA flood-MAR project design.

records.accounting_method:
(1) Causal impact verification: Bayesian structural time-series model (CausalImpact R package) generates a business-as-usual pumping scenario for 1996-2017 using covariates (precipitation, aridity, corn prices, year) calibrated to the pre-LEMA period (1996-2012); actual LEMA-period pumping (2013-2017) compared against the BAU posterior distribution to isolate the program effect while controlling for climate variability. A paired control region with matched well density, crop area, precipitation, and pumping density confirms that observed reductions are unique to SD-6.
(2) Conservation strategy partitioning: water savings attributed among three strategies using metered WIMAS pump records, satellite-derived annual irrigation maps (AIM, 30m Landsat), and USDA Cropland Data Layers — DPArea (savings from reduced irrigated area), DPDepth (savings from reduced per-crop irrigation depth, isolated via per-crop causal impact analysis), and DPCrop (savings from switching to less water-intensive crops).

records.key_finding: The SD-6 LEMA reduced groundwater pumping 31% relative to the business-as-usual scenario — exceeding the 20% target — with 72% of savings from improved irrigation efficiency, 19% from crop switching, and only 9% from reduced irrigated area, demonstrating that enforceable metered allocation accounting with carryover provisions can achieve significant demand reduction while farmers maintain irrigated area and net profit.

"To partition water savings among these three conservation strategies, we combined satellite-derived irrigated areas and crop type maps with well records. We found that farmers were able to largely maintain irrigated area and achieved the majority of pumping reductions (72%) from improvements in irrigation efficiency, followed by expansion of crops with lower water demand (19%)." "Increases in irrigation efficiency are often ineffective at reducing overall water consumption, but enforceable accounting, extraction limits, and improved understanding of irrigator behavior can help ensure efficiency improvements translate into water conservation." (Discussion, p. 9)
records.accounting_gap: The causal impact method requires high-quality, multi-decade metered pump records — a data infrastructure that Kansas has but most California GSAs lack. The method cannot yet account for changes in irrigation return flows that may offset apparent groundwater savings at the basin scale. Generalizability to larger LEMA scales or regions without strong local leadership remains untested.

However, Kansas's totalizing flowmeter infrastructure is likely more robust than CA GSAs.

Impacts of winter cover cropping on soil moisture and evapotranspiration in California's specialty crop fields may be minimal during winter months. California Agriculture, 76(1), 37–45.
records.geography: California Central Valley, USA — 10 commercial and UC research farms across Sacramento Valley (Davis, Dixon, Orland, Durham, Chico) and San Joaquin Valley (Five Points, Firebaugh, Merced, Arvin, Shafter); processing tomato fields and almond orchards
records.accounting_method:
(1) Soil moisture: neutron hydroprobe (Campbell Pacific Nuclear) measured volumetric soil water content at 0.15m to 2.7m depth in 0.30m increments from October to March/June 2016-2019; minimum four access tubes per treatment; gravimetric soil sampling (n=2,755) for neutron probe validation. T-tests conducted on 3,755 depth-date combinations to evaluate treatment significance. Fractional soil moisture calculated by normalizing neutron probe counts to maximum seasonal moisture to identify end-of-season soil moisture retention.
(2) Actual ET: residual energy balance (REB) method using surface renewal (SR) technique at Davis and Five Points (2017-2018 season only); latent heat flux (LE) calculated as residual of surface energy balance from micro-meteorological measurements; ETa compared against CIMIS ETo from nearest weather stations.
records.data_sources: Campbell Pacific Nuclear Model 503 neutron hydroprobe; gravimetric soil moisture (2,755 samples); surface renewal sonic anemometer equipment (REB method); CIMIS stations 6 (Davis) and 2 (Five Points); R software v3.6.0 for statistical analysis.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program. Study designed to provide empirical data for growers and GSAs facing uncertainty about cover crop water use under SGMA. Authors note the findings are representative of commercial farm conditions but caution that variability in management history, soil type, and precipitation limits generalizability.
records.key_finding: Seasonal cumulative ETa difference between winter cover cropped and bare ground was negligible at Davis (3mm) and Five Points (18mm), amounting to less than a single irrigation event and less than 10% of field ETo — directly contradicting the assumption underlying many GSA accounting frameworks that cover crops significantly increase CUgw relative to bare ground fallow.
records.direct_quotes:
"The difference in seasonal cumulative ETa between winter cover cropped and control ground is negligible in both Davis (3 mm) and Five Points (18 mm)... the water used by winter cover crops amounts to less than a single irrigation event (1 inch) and less than 10% of field ETo." (Results/Discussion, p. 43)

"Data sets of the surface energy balance parameters collected using micro-meteorological measurements were analyzed and the REB method was used to quantify the actual water losses (ETa) in winter cover cropped and control plots. We compiled and used three data types for the analyses: weather, pre-flux and energy balance data." (Methods, Data processing, p. 40)
records.accounting_gap: ETa measurements conducted at only two sites for one season — insufficient to characterize the full range of California cover crop ET variability across soil types, precipitation years, and cover crop species. The study did not formally partition ETa into precipitation-sourced versus groundwater-sourced ET, which is the specific quantity GSAs need for CUgw accounting. Soil moisture differences occurred primarily in the 0-120cm root zone, suggesting future studies only need to instrument this depth range.

Most current California-specific empirical ET measurement study for winter cover crops.

Neglible ETa finding (3-18mm) challenges the GSA accounting practice of treating cover crops as increasing CUgw.

However, no formal ET source split between precipitation and groundwater, which is what is needed for GAP cover crop crediting under SGMA.

records.citation: Dobbin, K.B. (2020). "Good Luck Fixing the Problem": Small Low-Income Community Participation in Collaborative Groundwater Governance and Implications for Drinking Water Source Protection. Society & Natural Resources, 33(12), 1468-1485. DOI: 10.1080/08941920.2020.1772925
records.geography: California; small low-income/disadvantaged communities across multiple Groundwater Sustainability Agency (GSA) basins
records.analysis_method: Semi-structured interviews examined how small, low-income communities participated in forming their local Groundwater Sustainability Agency and developing its Groundwater Sustainability Plan under the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act; transcripts coded via constant comparative method.
records.key_finding: Formal governance representation did not reliably predict actual engagement — some communities with no formal relationship to their Groundwater Sustainability Agency had representatives attending regularly, while some with formal seats attended less.
records.direct_quotes: "[These] social problems are not really caused by [the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act]. [The law] didn't create this at all, you know, it just created a container for a lot of it to be funneled in a very tight timeline." (Interview 25, Results)
records.learnings: Interviewees described concrete inequitable meeting dynamics — intimidation, self-censorship, being "talked down to," and differential treatment of farmers versus low-income Latino residents — that engagement design should actively work against. Letting participants choose the interview setting is a specific, low-cost access accommodation worth replicating. This is a diagnostic study (names barriers) rather than a prescriptive one — no itemized recommendations list.
records.community_selection: Sampling frame built from all small California census places (under 10,000 population) within basins covered by the Act, filtered to Disadvantaged Communities (median household income below 80% of the state median). 27 interviews with 35 people across 23 communities, averaging 43 minutes. Interview location chosen by the interviewee (homes, offices, community spaces, coffee shops) as a comfort accommodation. Spanish-language interviews offered but not ultimately used. No compensation reported.
records.notes:
Formal representation doesn't equal actual engagement.

Community member voting seat may be largely symbolic if decisions based on "majority rules".

Informational asymmetry was present: large water users informed about water governance reform more so than communities.

Community reps experienced inequitable meeting dynamics: intimidation, being "talked down to", differential treatment.

records.citation: Dobbin, K.B., Kuo, M., Lubell, M., et al. (2023). Drivers of (in)equity in Collaborative Environmental Governance. Policy Studies Journal, 51(2). DOI: 10.1111/psj.12483
records.geography: California, San Joaquin Valley (45 submitted Groundwater Sustainability Plans)
records.analysis_method: Not interview-based. Content-analyzed 45 Groundwater Sustainability Plans using a structured environmental justice scoring rubric (13 questions across 7 topics), then used gradient-boosted regression to test which factors predict three equity outcome measures.
records.key_finding:
Form"Representation" and "stakeholder engagement" are two separate categories in this paper, not one thing. That matters a lot:

Representation — formal structural measures like the percent of board members who are people of color, or the percent representing drinking water users — was the second most influential category overall, averaging 26% of predictive power, and in two of the three models it was the single strongest category.
Stakeholder engagement — generic measures like whether outreach happened or public comments were incorporated — was consistently the least influential category, at only 10%.
records.direct_quotes: "Problem severity/salience is the most influential factor representing 33.54% of the model explained variance whereas stakeholder engagement accounts for just less than a third of that influence (10.01% of cumulative relative influence)." (Results)
records.learnings: The environmental justice scoring rubric itself (covering representation, outreach quality, comment incorporation, and drinking water provisions) is a reusable instrument the Groundwater Accounting Platform team could adapt to self-score its own engagement design, even though the paper offers no interview-based recommendations.
records.community_selection: Not applicable — no primary recruitment, interview, or survey; unit of analysis is the submitted plan document.
records.notes:
Formal representation on a groundwater agency's governing board was a substantially stronger predictor of whether a plan addressed drinking water equity than generic stakeholder engagement or outreach activity, and even the strongest predictors produced only modest real-world change — leading the authors to caution against treating broad, non-required engagement efforts as a sufficient lever for equity on their own.

records.geography: Generic floodplain-aquifer system (numerical model domain); Murray-Darling Basin, Australia (analytical equation validation against HydroGeoSphere numerical model)
records.accounting_method: (1) Coupled numerical model: HydroGeoSphere fully coupled surface-subsurface flow model run with systematically varied parameters — clogging layer conductance (Kc: 0.001-10 m/day), flood wave height (0.5-5m), flood peak duration (1-100 days), aquifer transmissivity (1-10,000 m²/day), and hydraulic gradient toward river (0-0.001) — to identify controlling factors on flood recharge volumes across 1,000+ model runs. (2) Analytical equation derivation: dimensionless analysis identifies three limiting regimes (clogging-layer limited, storage limited, transmissivity limited); analytical equation Iactual = min(I, ΔS + Q) derived where I = potential infiltration (Darcy's law through clogging layer), ΔS = available storage above water table, Q = lateral aquifer outflow capacity (Darcy's law). (3) Validation: analytical equation results compared to HydroGeoSphere numerical model results across full parameter space; RMSE and bias calculated by limiting regime.
records.data_sources: HydroGeoSphere fully coupled surface-subsurface flow model (Therrien et al. 2006; Brunner and Simmons 2011); parametric sweep across clogging conductance, flood height, flood duration, aquifer transmissivity, and hydraulic gradient; analytical verification against 1,000+ numerical model scenarios.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program. Explicitly designed as a screening tool for use where detailed numerical modeling is not feasible. Authors state the analytical equation can be applied to 'estimate recharge at scales where numerical groundwater modeling is not warranted or applicable.'
records.key_finding: Clogging layer conductance is the single most important parameter controlling flood recharge — it sets an absolute upper bound on infiltration regardless of flood height or duration — and the analytical equation Iactual = min(I, ΔS + Q) predicts flood recharge volumes accurately across three distinct limiting regimes, providing a defensible screening-level tool for estimating recharge from flood events without requiring a calibrated numerical model.
records.direct_quotes:
"Recharge increased with clogging layer conductance, flood height, peak duration, and aquifer transmissivity. Recharge decreased with stronger groundwater gradients toward the river... A dimensionless analysis of the flood recharge process identified the factors that limited flood infiltration for each of the modeled scenarios: the clogging layer conductance, aquifer storage, and aquifer transmissivity." (Abstract/Results, p. 1)

"An analytical equation was derived to predict flood recharge in systems where complex numerical modeling is not warranted or applicable. Results from the analytical equation compared favorably with recharge modeled using a more complex numerical model." (Abstract, p. 1)
records.accounting_gap: Clogging layer conductance — the most important parameter — is extremely difficult to measure at field scale and highly spatially variable, making application of the analytical equation uncertain for real sites. Flood wave shape (rising vs. falling limb asymmetry) is not captured in the analytical formulation. The equation does not account for lateral flow on the floodplain surface or preferential flow paths through the clogging layer.

Provides an anlytical equation based on four physical parameters (conductance of clogging layer, flood wave height, flood peak duration and aquifer transmissivity) that could easily be plugged into GAP

records.geography: Intermountain West, USA (MT, ID, WY, OR, CO, NV, UT, AZ, NM)
records.accounting_method: Satellite-based spatial inventory of flood-irrigated grass-hay production combined with Landsat 8/9 surface water modeling (30m, 2013–2022 mean conditions) to classify wetland hydroperiods (temporary <2 months, seasonal 2–9 months, semi-permanent >9 months). Wetland hydroperiod classes used as indicators of ecosystem services including groundwater recharge. Grass-hay wetlands intersected with LANDFIRE pre-settlement riparian ecosystem maps to quantify overlap with historic riparian systems. Proportion of irrigated agriculture supporting grass-hay wetlands calculated using IrrMapper dataset. Elevation distributions compared across land use types.
records.data_sources: Landsat 8/9 Operational Land Imager (30m pixel, 2013–2022); IrrMapper Irrigated Lands dataset; USDA Cropland Data Layer (NASS); Rangeland Analysis Platform perennial grass cover (Allred et al. 2021); LANDFIRE Biophysical Settings (pre-Euro-American settlement ecological systems); USGS 10m National Elevation Dataset; Google and Sentinel-2 high-resolution imagery for on-screen delineation.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No operational crediting program. Authors explicitly identify this as the 'first-ever spatially explicit framework' linking grass-hay ranching to riparian ecosystem services. Results oriented toward informing regional conservation planning and policy discussions about irrigation efficiency transitions.
records.key_finding: Flood-irrigated grass-hay accounts for 57.8% of temporary and 19.9% of seasonal wetlands in the Intermountain West. Recharge and riparian ecosystem service co-benefits that are entirely unaccounted for in current irrigation efficiency policy frameworks.
records.direct_quotes:
"We estimated the proportion of irrigated agriculture supporting grass-hay wetlands in the Intermountain West using IrrMapper Irrigated Lands dataset. Calculations were made by dividing the area of grass-hay by the total area of irrigated land." (Methods, Section 2.4)

"We acknowledge that local ecological complexities can influence relationships between irrigation practices and ES benefits through variance in the mechanistic drivers underlying hydrologic function (i.e., geology, climate, and land use)." (Discussion)
records.accounting_gap: No existing accounting framework captures the groundwater recharge and riparian ecosystem service co-benefits of flood-irrigated grass-hay. Local ecological complexity (geology, climate, land use) means recharge co-benefits cannot be assumed from practice adoption alone — site-specific hydrologic attribution required. Irrigation efficiency policies treat flood irrigation as water waste without accounting for ecosystem service losses.
records.notes:
Most relevant to Cluster 6 framing in methods document.

Interesting but not sure how relevant for CA. Maybe something to keep in mind for expansion.

Not totally buying that grass-hay wetlands are the type of ecosystem we are looking for.

records.citation: Dybala, K.E., et al. (2025). Multiple-Benefit Conservation in Practice: A Framework for Quantifying Multidimensional Effects of Landscape Change in California's Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta. San Francisco Estuary and Watershed Science, 23(2).
records.geography: Sacramento–San Joaquin River Delta, California, USA (legal Delta boundary; baseline land cover as of 2018; three alternative landscape scenarios projected to 2050)
records.accounting_method:
(1) Four benefit categories quantified across three alternative landscapes (habitat restoration, perennial crop expansion, and combination): agricultural livelihoods (gross production value and FTE employment per ha by land cover class, from county CDFA data 2014-2020); water quality (pesticide application rates kg/ha/yr from CDPR 2014-2018 and crop-specific groundwater nitrogen loading kg N/ha/yr from Harter et al. 2017); climate-change resilience (Shannon diversity index plus qualitative drought/flood/heat tolerance scores per land cover); biodiversity support (boosted regression tree distribution models for 9 riparian landbird species and 6 waterbird groups applied to each alternative landscape).
(2) Net effect calculation: total landscape score SmL = Σ(mi × Ai) for each metric m and land cover class i; net effect dmL = SmL(alternative) - SmL(baseline); uncertainty estimated via standard error propagation for quantitative metrics and bootstrap resampling for biodiversity models.
(3) Open-source R package DeltaMultipleBenefits released to support extension to new metrics, alternative landscapes, and scenarios.
records.data_sources: 2018 baseline land cover (Dybala et al. 2023, 30m raster, modified from Schwenkler 2019); CDFA annual crop production value and acreage data 2014-2020 by county; CEDD agricultural employment data by county; CDPR pesticide use reports 2014-2018; Harter et al. (2017) crop-specific groundwater nitrogen loading rates; DWR InSAR subsidence data; Point Blue Water Tracker 2013-2019 open surface water probability; boosted regression tree bird distribution models (Dybala et al. 2023); Delta Plan habitat restoration targets and candidate restoration shapefiles; Wilson et al. (2021, 2022) perennial crop expansion projections.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program. Framework is designed as a scenario planning and trade-off analysis tool for California Delta management, not a post-implementation verification protocol. Authors explicitly frame alternative landscapes as illustrations of the framework's application rather than realistic 2050 scenarios, and explicitly state that no concurrent changes in environmental conditions, land management, or land cover quality are assumed.
records.key_finding: A flexible open-source multi-benefit accounting framework using per-hectare benefit metrics by land cover class, applied across alternative landscape scenarios with quantified uncertainty, can simultaneously track agricultural livelihood trade-offs, water quality improvements, climate resilience, and biodiversity support — providing a scalable template for multi-benefit attribution in MLRP project evaluation that GAP could adapt for the Central Valley context.
records.direct_quotes:
"To evaluate the net effects of each AL on each benefit category and metric, we first developed total landscape scores for each of the metrics... SmL = Σ(mi × Ai), where mi is the per-ha estimate for each metric m in each land-cover class i, n is the number of land-cover classes, and Ai is the total area of each land-cover class in the Delta in landscape L." (Methods, Evaluation of Alternative Landscapes, p. 9)

"To support the reproducibility of our analyses and their extension to new metrics, models, data sources, and alternative landscapes, we developed the customized R package 'DeltaMultipleBenefits'." (Methods, p. 9)
records.accounting_gap: Framework is prospective (scenario-based) rather than retrospective (post-implementation verification) — it projects what benefits a land use change would produce but does not verify what benefits were actually delivered. Water supply reliability — one of the Delta's two co-equal legal goals — is not included as a benefit metric in this iteration due to data limitations. No groundwater accounting component is included despite groundwater being central to the MLRP context. Framework assumes no change in per-hectare land cover quality or management intensity under alternative landscapes, which oversimplifies real-world restoration trajectories.
records.notes:
If GAP knows the area and land cover class of each MLRP project parcel, this framework provides a template for attributing multi-benefit scores across agricultural livelihoods, water quality, climate resilience, and biodiversity.

Open-source R package DeltaMultipleBenefits makes the framework immediately reproducible.

The Delta context does not include groundwater considerations — something that could be added for CV applications

records.geography: California Central Valley, USA (156 small DACs <15 km² — 126 in San Joaquin Valley, 33 in Sacramento Valley; 661,620 inhabitants)
records.accounting_method: (1) DAC selection and buffer analysis: 156 frontline DACs <15 km² identified using DWR median household income threshold (<80% statewide average); agricultural land use quantified inside communities and in 400-m and 1,600-m buffer zones using DWR land use data; water use, groundwater overdraft reduction, nitrogen leaching reduction, and pesticide reduction calculated per buffer zone using crop-specific coefficients. (2) Recharge suitability scoring: SAGBI index applied to identify suitable recharge soils within each buffer; communities scored by proximity to canal/river (crossed by, within 400m, within 1600m) combined with SAGBI rating to produce a composite recharge potential assessment for 156 DACs. (3) Economic co-benefit accounting: input-output IMPLAN model used to estimate direct and indirect (spillover) revenue and employment impacts of land retirement inside DACs and buffer zones under low and high investment scenarios for clean industry and solar energy repurposing alternatives.
records.data_sources: DWR land-water use data 2011–2015; CA EPA Pesticide Use Reports; nitrate (fertilizer) loading coefficients; DWR DAC designation data; SAGBI index (UC Davis); IMPLAN input-output economic model; ACS socio-economic data; DWR canal/river GIS layers.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No operational crediting program. Framework explicitly designed to 'influence and guide public policies in California around reducing the equity gap, mitigating climate change, and complying with SGMA.' Authors present it as a scalable decision support tool for policy prioritization — directly applicable to MLRP project scoring and siting.
records.key_finding: Retiring 287 km² of agricultural land inside 156 Central Valley DACs would reduce groundwater overdraft by ~87 hm³/year (3.9% of SJV annual overdraft) and cut nitrogen leaching by 2.6 Gg/year — and 89% of studied communities have moderately good or better MAR recharge potential within 1,600 m of a water source, demonstrating that a buffer-zone accounting framework can simultaneously quantify water, environmental, and economic co-benefits for DACs at a regional scale.
records.direct_quotes:
"We computed agricultural retirement for small (< 15 km²) frontline communities classified as disadvantaged according to the California Department of Water Resources (median household income less than 80% of that for the state's), using the surrounding 400-m (¼ of a mile) and 1600-m (1 mile) zones, referred to as buffers... we quantified the income and employment gains from repurposing part of the buffers into clean industry and solar energy generation and storage scenarios using plausible ranges of investment values, payback, and minimum acceptable rate of return." (Methods summary, p. 3)

"Net groundwater use reduction, which accounts for irrigation efficiency and irrigation water infiltration decrease, can contribute to reducing the groundwater overdraft in the San Joaquin Valley by roughly 87 hm³ per year inside disadvantaged communities (representing a reduction of 3.9% on the estimated annual overdraft), 156 hm³ in the 400-m buffer (7% reduction), and 809 hm³ in the 1600-m buffer (36.4%)." (Results, p. 4)
records.accounting_gap: Groundwater overdraft reduction estimates use net water use coefficients rather than hydrologic modeling — actual recharge benefits to specific domestic wells are not quantified. SAGBI-based recharge suitability does not incorporate groundwater flow direction or well capture zones, so the spatial connection between MAR site and benefiting DAC well is not established. Economic analysis is scenario-based with wide investment ranges, not a verified accounting of realized benefits.

DAC are ripe for recharge.

IMPLAN model used to estimate economic co-benefits of land retirement.

records.citation: Fienen, M.N., Bradbury, K.R., Kniffin, M., & Barlow, P.M. (2017). Depletion mapping and constrained optimization to support managing groundwater extraction. Groundwater, 55(4), 485–499.
records.geography: Little Plover River (LPR) basin, Central Sands Region, Wisconsin, USA (small agricultural watershed with documented ISW depletion below a legally mandated minimum flow)
records.accounting_method: (1) Depletion potential mapping: the groundwater model is run at each well's normal pumping rate and then again at a slightly increased rate; the resulting change in stream baseflow divided by the change in pumping produces a response factor for each well-stream pair, creating a map that shows which wells cause the greatest baseflow reduction per unit pumped. (2) Sequential pumping reduction: wells are ranked from highest to lowest depletion potential and turned off one by one in that order until simulated baseflow meets the legally mandated minimum flow, identifying the smallest number of high-impact wells requiring reduction. (3) Constrained optimization: a linear programming algorithm finds the combination of pumping reductions across all managed wells that restores the stream to its legal minimum while minimizing total pumping cut, with a design parameter controlling how much reduction any single well or well group can absorb. (4) K-means clustering: wells are grouped into 20 or 50 clusters by spatial proximity and similar depletion potential, reducing the number of decision variables in the optimization and improving computational efficiency.
records.data_sources: Three-dimensional MODFLOW-Newton model of LPR basin (100-foot cell resolution, 3 layers: Pleistocene sand/gravel and Cambrian sandstone); MODFLOW-GWM optimization package (Ahlfeld et al. 2005); FlowSource software for flow path visualization; soil-water-balance (SWB) recharge model; Wisconsin DNR baseflow measurements at four LPR gauges; 2013 high-capacity well pumping data from Wisconsin DNR; scikit-learn K-means clustering (Python).
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program. Framework developed in response to Wisconsin DNR regulatory authority to consider groundwater-surface water interactions when permitting high-capacity wells. Authors explicitly frame depletion potential mapping and constrained optimization as guidance tools for stakeholders and resource managers to evaluate tradeoffs — not a regulatory accounting mechanism. The Wisconsin approach was later modified by a state Attorney General opinion limiting DNR's authority.
records.key_finding: Depletion potential mapping reveals that reducing pumping by the volumetric flow rate of the baseflow deficit would not restore stream flow without targeting wells by depletion potential — the highest-ranked 13 wells (out of 324) account for sufficient reduction to restore baseflow to the mandated level, while a uniform 30% reduction across all wells requires far greater total pumping reduction for the same result.
records.direct_quotes:
"Depletion potential is the potential reduction in flows at constraint locations due to perturbations of pumping rates at specific locations in the system... the change in baseflow at stream location i due to pumping at well location j is calculated as RF_ij = (Q_stream,i(Q_well,j + delta_Q_well) - Q_stream,i(Q_well,j)) / delta_Q_well." (Methods, p. 491)

"Depletion potential maps show that not all wells equally impact the stream. The maps were helpful in explaining that not all wells impact streams to the same degree and consideration of depletion potential can guide which wells can be the focus for management discussions to have the greatest impact on flow." (Results, p. 494)
records.accounting_gap: Only pumping rates are changed as decision variables in available optimization software; land use and groundwater recharge changes are not linked to pumping reductions, introducing error in agricultural settings where irrigation and recharge are closely coupled. Steady-state depletion potential misses important seasonal dynamics. K-means clustering introduces subjectivity in choosing number of clusters. The framework does not quantify uncertainty in model parameters or forecasts.
records.notes:
Depletion potential mapping is useful ISW tool for GSA well permitting and demand management decisions.

Response factor approach builds on SDF from Barlow and Leake (2012), extends it to multi-well, multi-stream settings using a numerical model.

GAP could use MODFLOW model to generate depletion potential maps and run scenarios.

Wisconsin regulatory context is different from SGMA but the underlying methodology is transferable.

records.citation: Gardner-Frolick, R., Jain, S., Martinussen, N., Chambliss, S., Jackson, D., Zimmerman, N., & Giang, A. (2025). Incorporating Community Knowledge Into Analysis of Air Quality Monitoring Network Data. GeoHealth, 9(7). DOI: 10.1029/2025GH001378
records.geography: Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada; not California
records.analysis_method: Researchers combined a residents' association survey, citizen-science odor reports, and a community mapping event to identify air pollution sources and vulnerable locations, then built two versions of the same statistical air-quality model (a land-use regression) — one using only standard public data, and one adding the community-reported sources as model variables — to directly test whether the added community knowledge improved model accuracy.
records.key_finding: Adding community-reported knowledge to a technical model produced a measurable improvement in model accuracy for two of three pollutants studied, giving a rare quantified answer to whether incorporating community knowledge is worth the effort, not just whether it feels inclusive.
records.direct_quotes: "Comparing the traditional LUR to a 'community' LUR that uses community-reported air pollution sources, model fit was improved in the community LURs for NO2 and NOx." (Abstract/Results)
records.learnings: Turnout at the mapping event was a real limitation (half of RSVPs attended), and the authors recommend concrete fixes for future efforts: hosting a series of drop-in events rather than one session, providing childcare, and timing events to coincide with existing neighborhood gatherings to lower the barrier to participation.
records.community_selection: The mapping event drew 10 participants out of 20 who RSVP'd, about a year after air-quality sensors were installed in the neighborhood; the residents' association survey (conducted separately, before this study) drew about 170 respondents; the paper explicitly notes it did not collect participant demographic information, limiting its ability to assess representativeness.
records.notes:
Quantifies the accuracy payoff of incorporating community knowledge into a technical model.

Answers the "is this worth it" question behind the data-layer framing from the 7/28 meeting with Noa.

records.citation: Islam, N., Wallender, W.W., Mitchell, J., Wicks, S., & Howitt, R.E. (2006). A comprehensive experimental study with mathematical modeling to investigate the affects of cropping practices on water balance variables. Agricultural Water Management, 82(1–2), 129–147.
records.geography: UC West Side Research and Extension Center (WSREC), Central Valley of California, USA (Five Points, semi-arid; 0.03 km² site; 32 plots in tomato-cotton rotation; 4-year experiment September 1999 to October 2003)
records.accounting_method:
(1) Field measurement: volumetric SWC measured biweekly using field-calibrated Campbell Nuclear Model 503 neutron hydroprobe at 15cm and 30-240cm in 30cm increments; calibration equation y=158.01u+2521.1 (r²=0.99); four time series (TCCC, TCNC, CTCC, CTNC) averaging west and east plot measurements.
(2) MIKE SHE hydrologic model calibration: physically-based model solving one-dimensional Richards' equation for vadose zone and three-dimensional groundwater flow; PEST automated calibration optimizes soil hydraulic (θs, θr, α, n, Ks) and vegetation (ETact, interception, root distribution) parameters against observed SWC data; model simulates ETact, soil water recharge (SWR), and overland flow. Performance evaluated using coefficient of determination (COD). (3) Scenario analysis: calibrated model used to simulate water balance under four management scenarios — varying water table elevation (0.95-6.45m), rainfall-to-ET ratio (R/ETp 0.18-0.72), cover crop termination date (22 January to 19 March), and pre-irrigation scheduling.
records.data_sources: Campbell Pacific Nuclear neutron hydroprobe (biweekly 1999-2003); MIKE SHE physically-based hydrologic model; PEST parameter estimation software; measured rainfall and irrigation time series; ETp calculated via crop coefficient approach (Allen et al. 1998) with leaf area index and root depth from Islam (2004) and Borg and Grimes (1986); measured evaporation data for validation (Ayars, personal communication, 2004).
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program. Study designed as a research and management decision support tool for irrigation managers in California's Central Valley. Scenario analysis explicitly framed to assist managers in determining the suitability of cropping practices given regional water table elevation and climate conditions.
records.key_finding: MIKE SHE simulation shows cover crop ETact was higher than bare ground Eact across all four winters in both crop rotations, but the calibrated model demonstrates that terminating cover crops one month before senescence reduces ETact by up to 31% — providing a quantitative management threshold directly applicable to GSA cover crop crediting policy.
records.direct_quotes:
"The results indicate that the loss of water through ETact is reduced by as much as 31%, due to less transpiration (Tact), if the cover crops are terminated one month (02/19/02) before the senescence stage (03/19/02). However, no substantial decrease occurs when the termination date is earlier than a month before the senescence stage." (Results, Section 3.3.3, p. 145)

"A physical based hydrologic model, MIKE SHE, is chosen along with a calibration model, PEST, to simulate these processes... PEST adjusts MIKE SHE parameters until the fit between simulated SWC data and observations is optimized in the weighted least squares sense." (Methods, Section 2.2, p. 194)
records.accounting_gap: Model-simulated ETact and SWR are not directly verified against independent ET measurements — validation is conducted only against soil water content, meaning ET and recharge partitioning carry unquantified uncertainty. Crop rotation effect on SWS was larger than cover cropping practice effect, suggesting that baseline calculation methodology (what crop preceded the cover crop) materially affects the accounting result. Study predates satellite ET tools, so no assessment of whether OpenET or LandIQ can detect the model-predicted ETact differences.
records.notes:
Cited as the primary basis for the SC Cover Crop SGMA Report's conservative 1.2-inch ET increase estimate.

31% ET reduction from early termination is the most actionable management finding for GSA crediting policy.

The scenario analysis structure (water table depth, aridity, termination date, pre-irrigation timing) maps directly onto the variables GAP would need to parameterize for site-specific cover crop water accounting.

Note: model-based findings, not direct field ET measurements.

records.citation: Jelks, N.O., Hawthorne, T.L., Dai, D., Fuller, C.H., & Stauber, C. (2018). Mapping the Hidden Hazards: Community-Led Spatial Data Collection of Street-Level Environmental Stressors in a Degraded, Urban Watershed. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 15(4), 825. DOI: 10.3390/ijerph15040825
records.geography: Proctor Creek Watershed, Northwest Atlanta, Georgia; not California
records.analysis_method: Ten resident "watershed researchers," partnered with Georgia State University faculty and students, applied an indicator-inclusion framework (rating candidate concerns against criteria including policy relevance) to narrow a broad set of environmental concerns down to three specific, mappable stressors, then co-designed a mobile GIS app to collect structured point, photo, and descriptive data on those stressors, later analyzed for statistically significant spatial clustering.
records.key_finding: A structured indicator-selection process narrowed open-ended resident concerns into a small number of specific, quantifiable, policy-relevant data layers, and the resulting community-generated dataset filled a documented gap in publicly available environmental hazard data for the watershed.
records.direct_quotes: "Unlike many GIS projects, the database design was controlled by the community research participants. Local knowledge and technical mapping expertise came together to enact a community plan that included collaborative design of the app, community-led data collection, and co-interpretation of the findings." (Discussion)
records.learnings: The authors flag real bias risk in what gets mapped, driven by residents' own judgment of significance — for example, illegal dumping was underrepresented in the data specifically because it was so common that individual instances felt unworthy of separately logging; future efforts should account for this kind of participant subjectivity when designing the data-collection protocol.
records.community_selection: Residents recruited via flyers in community parks, recreation centers, and health clinics, plus face-to-face contact at neighborhood association meetings, with snowball sampling to reach a target of 10 participants (ages 29-66, 8-66 years' residency) representing the watershed's primary neighborhood planning units; residents were paired with university teams into five field teams for structured data collection over two data-collection phases.
records.notes: No California context, but the indicator-narrowing framework (broad concerns to a short list of mappable, policy-relevant indicators) is one of the most directly transferable methods in the review for GAP's own "what data layers do communities need" question.

records.geography: Fairmead, Madera County, California (San Joaquin Valley; unincorporated severely disadvantaged community, median household income below 60% of the state's)
records.analysis_method: A commentary/case narrative (not a coded empirical evaluation) co-written by the nonprofit, community, farmer, and researcher partners describing the multi-year Fairmead Groundwater Resilience Project: six community workshops (2022-2025, attendance 10-60) that moved from identifying community needs to co-designing a specific Multibenefit Land Repurposing Program (MLRP) project on a willing farmer's land, plus the water-savings and flood-capacity metrics calculated for that project once designed.
records.key_finding: The engagement process directly produced the accounting inputs for an MLRP project — the specific water-savings figure (37.6 AF/year) reported for this project was calculated after community workshops had already selected the project type and located a willing landowner, not before, meaning community engagement here functioned as a front-end siting/selection mechanism feeding into project-level accounting rather than a downstream communication step.
records.direct_quotes:
"Coming into the community as an external party, it was also important that the team respect the community's preferences without pushing a predetermined agenda or set of goals." (Section 3.4.1)

"For this 17.3-acre almond orchard, the average annual water used was 53 acre-feet (AF)... After native vegetation restoration, the average annual water used will be 15.4 AF... saving 37.6 AF... of water per year." (Section 3.3)
records.learnings: Farmer recruitment was the binding constraint on turning community-identified priorities into an actual repurposing project, not community interest — of the priorities generated in the first three workshops (water security, air quality, park/community space, ecosystem restoration, flood reduction), only the subset a landowner was willing to implement on their land became the funded project. The five "keys to success" the authors name (integrate local knowledge, provide ongoing education, use effective outreach, encourage participation, be a flexible partner) are practitioner-reported, not evaluated against a comparison case.
records.community_selection: Self-selected workshop attendees recruited through the local nonprofit Fairmead Community & Friends (FCF), door-to-door canvassing with trusted community leaders, bilingual (English/Spanish) flyers, and outreach at existing community events; no formal sampling frame, no compensation reported beyond food and raffles at workshops. Farmer participation required separate, harder-won recruitment (mailers, door-to-door, personal follow-up) described as the most difficult part of the process.
records.notes:
Not California-wide or SGMA-representative — a single-project case study from one nonprofit-led effort, useful for concrete engagement tactics rather than generalizable findings.

Direct empirical bridge between Community Considerations and MLRP accounting: shows what a community-driven land-repurposing project's input-side numbers (acres, AF saved, flood-basin capacity) look like when the accounting is downstream of a participatory siting process rather than assigned top-down.
