records.citation: Koebele, E.A., Méndez-Barrientos, L.E., Nadeau, N., Gerlak, A.K. (2023). Beyond engagement: Enhancing equity in collaborative water governance. WIREs Water, 11(2), e1687. DOI: 10.1002/wat2.1687
records.geography: California (SGMA groundwater governance case) and the transnational Colorado River Delta (United States-Mexico); not a California-only study
records.analysis_method: An advanced literature review, not an empirical study. The authors synthesize collaborative-governance scholarship into four recurring "design features" (diverse actor engagement, deliberation, iterative interactions, consensus orientation), each scored against three components of equity (recognitional, procedural, distributional), then apply the framework to two published case studies — SGMA groundwater governance reform and the Minute 319/323 Colorado River Delta process — drawn from existing literature rather than new fieldwork.
records.key_finding: Recognitional equity (who is at the table) is the easiest of the three equity types to achieve and is not sufficient on its own — the SGMA case shows collective GSAs that engaged diverse actors for the first time still let large public agencies dominate deliberation, and some GSAs imposed financial requirements for voting seats that caused low-resourced actors to disengage over time.
records.direct_quotes: "...the four design features we identified should be considered together because they are mutually reinforcing: even when more diverse representation is achieved, failing to acknowledge and address procedural and distributional inequities, in addition to persistent gaps in representation, will undermine the ability of collaborative water governance processes to develop solutions that fairly address complex water sustainability problems." (Conclusion)
records.learnings: The four design features interact rather than operating independently — a consensus-orientation requiring "greater-than-majority" agreement, found in most of the 74 collective GSAs studied by Moran et al. (2019), signals inclusiveness but can also let powerful actors veto broadly-supported but contested actions, silencing less powerful voices. The authors found almost no evidence on distributional equity (who actually benefits or bears burdens) for either case, because implementation outcomes take years to materialize and are hard to attribute to a governance process specifically — a gap GAP could help close by tracking outcomes over time, not just process participation.
records.community_selection: Not applicable — a conceptual/comparative review built from published case-study literature, not a primary study with its own participant recruitment.
records.notes:
Framework paper, not a data source — useful for structuring how GAP's Community Considerations documentation distinguishes "who was invited" from "who could actually influence the outcome" from "who benefited."

Cites Bostic et al. (2022, in "Further Reading," distinct from Bostic et al. 2023 already in this tab): preliminary modeling of draft GSPs predicted inequitable drinking-water impacts to domestic and public supply wells — an early version of the same well-failure finding.

records.citation: Kourakos, G., Dahlke, H.E., & Harter, T. (2019). Increasing groundwater availability and seasonal base flow through agricultural managed aquifer recharge in an irrigated basin. Water Resources Research, 55(9), 7464–7492.
records.geography: Orland-Artois Water District (OAWD), Colusa groundwater subbasin, Northern California Central Valley (~0.34 million acres; bounded by Coast Range, Sacramento River, and Stony Creek)
records.accounting_method:
(1) C2VSim scenario modeling: C2VSim (California Central Valley Groundwater-Surface Water Simulation Model, IWFM-based, DWR) run over 88 years (1922–2009) with 320 Ag-MAR scenarios varying diversion point (Stony Creek vs. Sacramento River), recharge location (4 spatial distributions), recharge target amount (8 depths/volumes, 10–381 TAF/year), and recharge timing (5 seasonal windows).
(2) Groundwater storage accounting: ΔSc(t) = Σj=1t Σk=1Nel ΔSj,k : cumulative monthly difference in groundwater storage between Ag-MAR scenario and base case across all C2VSim finite elements.
(3) Base flow accounting: ΔBc(t) = −Σj=1t Σk=1Nel ΔQsa,j,k : cumulative change in net groundwater discharge to streams (stream-aquifer flux difference between scenario and base). Recharge water partitioned between groundwater storage and base flow gains over time.
records.data_sources: C2VSim fine grid (32,537 finite elements; 3-layer aquifer system; calibrated 1975–2003 against groundwater heads, vertical head differences, and surface water flows using PEST); SAGBI index for Ag-MAR site selection (Moderately Good/Good/Excellent soils only); 2014 USDA NASS Cropland Data Layer (land use constraint — alfalfa and almond fields only); DWR groundwater level measurements (478 wells, spring 2009); USGS gage 11389500 (Sacramento River flows); OAWD water management data.
records.formal_program_or_crediting:
No formal crediting program.
Framework designed to demonstrate how large-scale integrated modeling (C2VSim) can support water management decisions about Ag-MAR design (diversion point, timing, and location) and their effects on groundwater storage and base flow.
Authors note operational constraints (water rights, environmental flow minimums, infrastructure limits) not included in modeling must be addressed in actual implementation.
records.key_finding: Across all 320 Ag-MAR scenarios, diverted water split approximately 34% to groundwater storage and 66% to base flow returns over 80 years. But during the first 20 years, 60–70% went to storage; base flow benefits are delayed and grow continuously over decades, buffered by aquifer storage against seasonal and interannual variability in recharge.
records.direct_quotes:
"In all scenarios the diverted water was split into groundwater storage (about 34%) or return flow to streams (about 66%). During the first decades of Ag‐MAR operation the diverted water contributed mainly to groundwater storage (60–70% in the first 20 years). In the OAWD study basin, given its size and hydrogeology, Ag‐MAR takes over a century to reach a new dynamic groundwater storage equilibrium, regardless of recharge scenario." (Conclusions, p. 7488)

"The cumulative base flow gains equal the difference between cumulative recharge and groundwater storage change... Base flow gains, however, are buffered against these highly variable groundwater inflows by aquifer storage between the recharge area and the stream network." (Results, Section 3.2, p. 7478)
records.accounting_gap: C2VSim does not constrain pumping as a function of groundwater levels, so changes in groundwater storage from Ag-MAR do not directly reduce pumping in the model — overstating net storage gains. Vadose zone travel time and additional crop ET from elevated water tables not simulated — affects accuracy of near-term benefit accounting. Environmental flow minimums and downstream water rights not incorporated — 'best case' scenarios only. 88-year simulation period insufficient to reach new dynamic equilibrium in large basins.
records.notes:
If C2VSim runs are available for a GSA, GAP could track storage-to-baseflow ration over time and use it for ISW co-beenfits to ag-MAR projects.

Does not provide a method for attributing base flow gains at a specific stream reach to a specific recharge project (only subbassin scale under idealized conditions).

Decadal lag before baseflow benefits materialize is the main accounting challenge (GSAs cannot attribute recharge to baseflow contribution right away).

C2VSim is DWR's own model, so this framework is directly compatible with the modeling infrastructure GAP operates within. Authors (Dahlke, Harter) are UC Davis faculty central to the SGMA technical community.

records.citation: Marwaha, N., Kourakos, G., Levintal, E., & Dahlke, H.E. (2021). Identifying agricultural managed aquifer recharge locations to benefit drinking water supply in rural communities. Water Resources Research, 57(3), e2020WR028811.
records.geography: Southern Central Valley, California, USA (288 rural DACs across Kings, Kern, Tulare, Fresno counties; 20,820 km²)
records.accounting_method:
(1) Ag-MAR suitability: SAGBI index (five soil factors: deep percolation, root zone residence time, topography, chemical limitations, surface condition) identifies land ranked Excellent/Good/Moderately Good; combined with land use (annuals, vineyards, fallowed fields) and proximity to conveyance infrastructure using unique distance buffers per infrastructure type.
(2) Domestic well capture zones: C2VSim finite element model (average element 2.6 km²) provides quasi-steady-state regional groundwater flow field (mean of October 2005–September 2015 monthly flows); particle tracking applied to identify the upgradient recharge area contributing to each of 7,673 domestic wells within 1.61 km of 288 rural communities.
(3) Community vulnerability index: composite score combining domestic well failures (2012–2016 drought, self-reported), domestic well reliance, pesticide applications, land subsidence (InSAR, 90m raster), and socio-economic factors (poverty status, linguistic isolation, educational attainment from ACS block groups) to prioritize Ag-MAR locations by community need.
records.data_sources: SAGBI index (UC Davis); DWR Statewide Crop Mapping 2014; surface water conveyance GIS data from nine water management agencies; C2VSim-FG groundwater model (DWR); OSWCR well completion reports (27,482 wells screened to 7,673); CA Household Water Supply Shortage Reporting System (867 reported dry wells in study area 2012–2016); NASA JPL InSAR subsidence raster (May 2015–September 2016, 90m); ACS Census block group data 2015; CA Department of Pesticide Regulation Pesticide Use Reports.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No operational crediting program. Framework designed as a decision support tool for water managers and GSAs to prioritize Ag-MAR investments by DAC benefit. Authors identify 2,998 agricultural land parcels within domestic well capture zones of 149 communities as candidate recharge sites.
records.key_finding: By spatially constraining Ag-MAR site selection within groundwater model-derived domestic well capture zones and weighting candidate sites by a composite DAC vulnerability index, the study identified 2,998 agricultural parcels across 149 of 288 rural communities where targeted recharge would most directly benefit drinking water supply. Demonstrates an operational spatial attribution method for recharge-to-DAC benefit accounting.
records.direct_quotes:
"Groundwater well capture zones are defined as the areal extent and volumetric portion of a groundwater system that contribute discharge to a particular well... Captures zones were derived for all domestic wells in rural communities using the California Department of Water Resources' Online System for Well Completion Reports (OSWCR) and the California Central Valley Groundwater-Surface Water Simulation Model (C2VSim)." (Methods, Section 3.1.2)

"To determine community vulnerability to change in groundwater supply, data describing domestic well failures, domestic well reliance, pesticide applications, land subsidence, and socio-economic factors were used." (Methods, Section 3.1.3)
records.accounting_gap: Well capture zones assume a quasi-steady-state regional flow field. However, transient recharge dynamics (e.g., seasonal or episodic flood-MAR events) are not captured. Self-reported well failure data significantly underestimates actual water supply shortages in rural communities. Vulnerability index weights are assigned without formal sensitivity analysis, introducing subjectivity into prioritization.
records.notes:
Co-benefits of recharge for DAC. Most directly applicable to GAP of all four DAC papers.

The capture zone + vulnerability index methodology is a ready-made spatial accounting framework for attributing recharge project benefits to specific DACs and their domestic rural wells.

The C2VSim model to estimate the gw flow is DWR's and already used in SGMA.

Community-Based Participatory Geographic Information Systems: Informing a Long-Term Drinking Water Research Collaboration. Annals of the American Association of Geographers, 116(4), 981-1002. DOI: 10.1080/24694452.2025.2601315
records.geography: Tennessee, statewide; not California
records.analysis_method: Over a six-year university-state-utility collaboration, researchers combined community-based participatory research with participatory GIS methods (a hybrid they name "CBPGIS") to co-produce a missing statewide dataset — spatial service-area boundaries for small drinking water systems — by holding recurring virtual work sessions where local water-system staff supplied on-the-ground spatial knowledge public records lacked, standardizing map formats, and running a structured verification process to resolve data-quality issues like overlapping boundaries.
records.key_finding: A dataset that had sat at only about 15% complete after a prior decade-long effort reached 98% completion once the project shifted from a purely technical data-collection approach to one built on sustained trust-building with the people who actually held the missing spatial knowledge.
records.direct_quotes: "The CBPGIS approach ensured trust was established with local spatial knowledge stakeholders to obtain the necessary information to coproduce 97 percent of the [community water system] service area boundary data for populations of 3,300 or less; only nine U.S. states have comparable data at this level." (Abstract)
records.learnings: The study built a verification protocol to catch predictable data-quality problems (like overlapping service areas) that emerged from combining inconsistent data supplied by different local offices, and its "research competency model" for training students in this work could double as an onboarding structure for anyone new to GAP's own data-coproduction work.
records.community_selection: Stakeholders were state environmental and health agency staff, a state water-utility association, and community water system representatives, working alongside 13 student research assistants (nine undergraduates, four graduate students); the team explicitly used a team-development framework (forming, storming, norming, performing) to build trust before attempting the technical data work.
records.notes:
Likely too large a scale to replicate, but this is the clearest evidence in the review that a well-designed trust-building process to close a longstanding water data gap.

records.geography: Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, CA (Legal Delta and Delta Service Area), water years 2015-2016
records.analysis_method: Compares seven independent ET estimation methods against each other and against field measurements (eddy covariance and surface renewal stations at 14 field sites) across two water years; methods span crop-coefficient/water-balance and energy-balance/remote-sensing families
records.accounting_method: Crop-coefficient/water-balance models (CalSIMETAW, DETAW, SIMS); energy-balance remote-sensing methods (DisALEXI, ITRC-METRIC, UCD-METRIC, UCD-PT); direct field measurement (eddy covariance, surface renewal stations)
records.key_finding:
- Most comprehensive method comparison in this set: 7 methods head-to-head, spanning both accounting families (crop-coefficient/water-balance vs. remote sensing/energy-balance)
- Methods still diverge ~11% from ensemble mean even after standardization and calibration - quantifies the real cost of method choice
- Remote-sensing methods systematically overestimate ET relative to field measurements, worse in winter/cloudy conditions
- Report's own conclusion explicitly ties accurate ET estimation to SGMA basin water budgets and endorses remote sensing as a useful tool
- Central policy recommendation calls for a coordinated, pooled-funding statewide ET consortium rather than one-off comparisons - a direct parallel to GAP's own mission

records.citation: Megdal, S.B., Dillon, P., & Seasholes, K. (2014). Water banks: Using managed aquifer recharge to meet water policy objectives. Water, 6(6), 1500–1514.
records.geography: Arizona Active Management Areas (AMAs): Phoenix, Tucson, Pinal, Prescott, Santa Cruz — covering the majority of Arizona's population and irrigated agriculture
records.accounting_method:
(1) Permitting system: three independent permits required — storage facility permit (operation), water storage permit (right to store; required to accrue credits), and recovery well permit (right to withdraw). Permits require evaluation of hydrologic feasibility via numerical groundwater flow models, groundwater mounding assessment, and water quality compliance.
(2) Direct recharge accounting: deliveries reported to ADWR; monitor wells at recharge facilities track water levels and quality; evaporation losses calculated and excluded from eligible credits; 5% cut-to-the-aquifer applied to water left in storage beyond the calendar year (5% cannot be recovered — intended to augment regional aquifer storage).
(3) In-lieu recharge (groundwater savings): party supplying CAP water or effluent in lieu of groundwater pumping receives credit equal to the volume of groundwater that would otherwise have been pumped; Groundwater Savings Facility (GSF) permit required; credits legally identical to direct recharge credits.
(4) Recovery mass-balance: volume recharged equals volume authorized for future recovery; recovery can occur in a different location from recharge provided it is within the AMA and in an area not experiencing rapid groundwater decline (>1.22 m/year average decline threshold).
records.data_sources: ADWR Underground Storage and Recovery Program records; CAP water delivery records; AWBA annual reports (storage volumes, credit balances, firming targets); numerical groundwater flow models for hydrologic feasibility evaluation; monitor well networks at permitted recharge facilities.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: Fully operational formal crediting program. Arizona Underground Storage and Recovery Program has operated continuously since the mid-1980s, with the LTSC framework refined in 1994. As of the paper's publication, the AWBA alone had accrued more than 3,947 MCM (3.2 MAF) of LTSCs across Phoenix, Tucson, and Pinal AMAs toward a 4,493 MCM (3.643 MAF) firming target. LTSCs are freely transferable by simple account transfer. ADWR administers a centralized accounting database tracking every cubic meter stored and credited.
records.key_finding: Arizona's recharge crediting system demonstrates that formal MAR accounting requires at minimum: quantified water rights as a precondition, a three-permit system separating facility operation from storage rights from recovery rights, explicit accounting for evaporative losses and a permanent cut-to-the-aquifer, and a mass-balance recovery framework that allows spatial separation between recharge and recovery — the closest operational analog to what SGMA-aligned California recharge crediting would need to look like.
records.direct_quotes:
"In addition to permitting a recharge project itself, those proposing to store water must obtain a separate permit from ADWR, and must establish the legal right to source water. There are also reporting requirements for deliveries and both water levels and water quality from monitor wells at direct recharge facilities. To further ensure that only the volume of water added to the aquifer is eligible for recovery, losses due to evaporation are calculated and excluded." (Methods/Results, Section 2.3.3, p. 1505)

"The regulatory accounting then authorizes an equivalent amount of pumping to occur. The 'recovered' water may be hydrologically distinct from the recharge activity, but it retains the legal characteristic of the source water that was stored." (Results, Section 2.3.4, p. 1505)
records.accounting_gap: The mass-balance recovery framework — where pumping authorized anywhere in the AMA is treated as equivalent to recharged water — creates a spatial mismatch between the physical location of recharge benefits (aquifer storage, GDE support, domestic well recovery) and the location of credited water recovery. Over extended periods this hydrological mismatch can be detrimental. The paper acknowledges this but frames it as a policy tradeoff enabling broader program participation rather than a flaw to be solved.
records.notes:
Most detailed peer-reviewed description of a formal recharge crediting system in the western US.

The three-permit architecture (facility, storage, recovery) and the 5% cut-to-the-aquifer are the two most transferable design elements for California.

In-lieu recharge crediting mechanism related to SGMA-era demand management programs.

records.citation: Meyer, N., Bergez, J.-E., Constantin, J., & Justes, E. (2019). Cover crops reduce water drainage in temperate climates: A meta-analysis. Agronomy for Sustainable Development, 39(1), 3.
records.geography: Temperate climates (Köppen-Geiger classes B, C, D) — USA, France, Spain, UK, Ireland, Italy, Canada; 28 studies selected from 436 identified records; no California-specific studies included
records.accounting_method:
(1) Five-step meta-analysis following Philibert et al. (2012): Web of Science search (27 Sept 2017) using cover crop AND drainage query; 436 papers identified, 122 screened by full text, 28 selected meeting inclusion criteria; inclusion required drainage measured at ≥90cm depth, comparison to fallow bare soil, cover crops sown summer/autumn and terminated before next cash crop, field measurements (lysimeters/drained plots) or soil-crop model outputs, temperate climate.
(2) Effect size calculation: difference in drainage D = XCC - XBS per study-year; individual effect size Di = mean difference; standard deviation σDi calculated per study; 95% confidence interval CI95% = [Di - 1.96σD, Di + 1.96σD].
(3) Random-effects model: weighted mean effect size μRE = Σ(wi×Di)/Σwi where wi = 1/(σ²i + σ²b); heterogeneity tested via Q statistics; sensitivity analysis via AIC comparison of four statistical models; publication bias assessed via funnel plot. Separate meta-analyses for field measurement studies (n=22) and modeling studies (n=10).
records.data_sources: Web of Science database (27 Sep 2017); 32 studies (28 papers, four divided into paired field-model cases); WebPlotDigitizer for data extraction from figures; R software 'metafor' package, 'rma' function, REML method (Viechtbauer 2010); data extracted: drainage volumes under CC and bare soil, soil texture class, geographic location, annual precipitation, cover crop sowing season, cover crop biomass.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program. Authors frame drainage reduction as both a service (reduces nitrate leaching to groundwater) and a potential disservice (reduces groundwater recharge) depending on management context. No GSA-level or regulatory crediting mechanism described.
records.key_finding: Cover crops reduce water drainage by a mean of 27mm (field measurements) to 32mm (modeling) compared to bare soil across 32 studies, but no single factor — soil texture, precipitation level, sowing season, or biomass — was statistically significant in explaining variability, meaning the drainage reduction effect cannot be predicted from site characteristics alone without local measurement.
records.direct_quotes:
"To be included in the meta-analysis, papers had to fulfill all of the following criteria: (1) Contain data on water drainage, which we defined as water unavailable to plant roots and likely to recharge groundwater, i.e., measured at a depth of 90 cm or more; (2) Compare the impact of cover crops to that of fallow bare soil, without plant cover." (Methods, Section 2.1, p. 3)

"Cover crops reduce drainage compared to that of bare soil: the mean effect size of the meta-analysis was −27 mm for studies based on measurements and −32 mm for studies based on modeling. The 95% confidence interval of the effect size was very close: 20–34 mm for studies based on measurements." (Results, Section 3.2, p. 6)
records.accounting_gap: All 28 studies are from temperate Europe and North America — no California or Mediterranean-climate studies included, severely limiting direct transfer to SGMA contexts. No significant explanatory factors found for variability in drainage reduction, meaning a site-specific prediction of recharge impact from cover cropping is not possible from this literature. Study does not address whether drainage reduction represents a net water accounting benefit or cost under California's overdrafted conditions.

Winter cover crops consume precip that bare groundw ould have drained to aquifer (~27mm) meaning cover crops convert potential recharge into ET rather than drawing from gw.

GSA may apply same precip assumptions to cover crop and bare groudn—misassigning cover crop precip use as gw consumption.

Studies come from temperature Europe and North America, no CA or meditteranean.

records.citation: Morrisett, C.N., Van Kirk, R.W., & Null, S.E. (2024). Leveraging water rights and reservoir operations for agricultural managed aquifer recharge in a warming, water-scarce western watershed. Water Resources Research, 60(8), e2023WR036648.
records.geography: Henrys Fork watershed, upper Snake River Basin, Idaho, USA (8,300 km2; snow-dominated, spring-fed; fully adjudicated prior appropriation system with conjunctive groundwater-surface water management)
records.accounting_method: (1) Climate-based streamflow simulation: statistical regression models for five subwatersheds generate 1,000 independent 30-year daily streamflow time series (water years 2023-2052) incorporating observed climate trends; 1,000 replications capture stochastic variability in future water supply. (2) Integrated reservoir operations-hydrology model: daily model routes simulated streamflow through reservoirs, irrigation diversions, and minimum instream flow targets using prior appropriation water rights priority rules to produce site-specific Ag-MAR diversion volumes at five current and potential recharge sites across 30,000 total simulation years. (3) Groundwater-surface water response functions: site-specific response functions derived from Idaho's Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer Model (ESPAM 2.2) translate daily Ag-MAR diversion volumes into daily streamflow return flows at the target reach (Ashton-Rexburg). Steady-state streamflow response to Ag-MAR tabulated per site (Table 1) ranging from 48.8% to 71.8% of recharged volume returning to the target reach.
records.data_sources: Idaho ESPAM 2.2 regional groundwater model (1.6 km2 grid cells, Idaho Department of Water Resources); USGS streamflow gage 13056500 (Henrys Fork at Ashton); hydrometeorologic station data (water years 1989-2022, 12 stations); stakeholder-developed seasonal operations model (Joint Committee, 2018; Van Kirk, 2017b); Idaho water rights priority records; Egin Lakes and St. Anthony Union Canal infrastructure specifications; 2013-2023 observed Ag-MAR diversion records.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: Partial operational example. Idaho's fully adjudicated water rights system provides a formal legal framework for managed versus incidental recharge operations with documented water rights priority. The integrated reservoir-hydrology model is based on a stakeholder operations model actively used since 2017 for annual irrigation season planning. However, no formal crediting program for ISW co-benefits exists. Authors explicitly frame Ag-MAR for return flow recovery as an emerging management tool requiring expanded investigation.
records.key_finding: Site-specific groundwater-surface water response functions from a regional aquifer model show that 62% of total recharged water returned to the target reach annually at steady state, with summer low-flow periods (July-August) receiving a 6%-14% streamflow increase — demonstrating that response functions calibrated to a regional model can attribute specific streamflow gains to specific recharge sites under real water rights constraints.
records.direct_quotes:
"We input daily recharge availability into site-specific streamflow response functions from the state of Idaho's regional groundwater model to produce 30-year daily streamflow gain from aquifer recharge." (Methods, Section 2.2, p. 4)

"On average, our model demonstrated Ag-MAR operations reduced the springtime streamflow peak at the watershed outlet by 10%-14% and caused the runoff peak to occur up to 2 days earlier... However, on average, 62% of total recharged water returned to the target reach annually." (Results, Section 3.3, p. 11)
records.accounting_gap: Response functions assume linear aquifer response and steady-state conditions, which may not hold during transient recharge events or in highly overdrafted basins. Site suitability assessment (SAGBI, capture zone analysis) was outside scope, meaning recharge site locations were not formally evaluated for maximum return flow efficiency. Climate projections use a business-as-usual trend extrapolation rather than scenario-based GCM projections, introducing uncertainty in future water availability estimates. Incidental recharge via flood irrigation dominates return flow but is contingent on maintaining flood irrigation practices under agricultural transition pressures.
records.notes:
Response functions from regional aquifer models can attribute specific streamflow gains to specific recharge sites with seasonal timing.

Paper focus on water rights administration and return flow recovery more so thatn accounting design.

A participatory approach for developing a geospatial toolkit for mapping the suitability of California's Multibenefit Land Repurposing Program (MLRP) in support of groundwater sustainability. Frontiers in Water.
records.geography: Kaweah and Tule groundwater subbasins, San Joaquin Valley, California (Kaweah: 178,478 ha, population 339,000; Tule: 193,269 ha, population 95,000; both SGMA high-priority, both MLRP block grant recipients)
records.accounting_method:
(1) Six suitability indices constructed using fuzzy logic normalization (0 to 1 scale, linear or raised cosine functions based on empirical cumulative distribution): agricultural socioeconomic factors (weighted average of revenues 0.25, employment 0.25, applied water rate 0.50 — weights adjusted to ensure high-water-use lands score highest); managed aquifer recharge potential (proximity to water conveyance 0.25, SAGBI surficial soils 0.1875, AEM/CVHM subsurface coarse fraction 0.375, dry well density and InSAR subsidence 0.1875); renewable energy; habitat and wildlife corridor connectivity; flood risk reduction; and environmental health risk mitigation.
(2) All datasets aggregated to Public Land Survey System 1-mile grid (1.6 km resolution) to balance granularity and landowner privacy.
(3) Indices combined through weighted averages into a unified MLRP suitability heat map displayed in an interactive R Shiny web application, with user-adjustable weighting by objective (conservation vs. employment vs. community benefit).
(4) Participatory validation: iterative stakeholder workshops with MLRP project managers, NGOs, farmers, and community members used to validate dataset selection, threshold values, and weighting schemes across both subbasins.
records.data_sources: DWR 2022 Agricultural Land Use map; USDA crop revenue data; IMPLAN input-output employment model; DWR applied water rates by crop type; SAGBI index (O'Geen et al. 2015); DWR Airborne Electromagnetic (AEM) survey (2024, 0-33m depth); USGS CVHM subsurface texture model (to 38m); DWR dry well occurrence database (2014-present); DWR InSAR land subsidence raster (Sentinel-1A, 2015-2023, 2.5km); DWR streams and canals GIS shapefile; R packages: lfl (fuzzy logic), Shiny (interactive visualization).
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting or water savings verification program. Tool is explicitly a siting and prioritization decision support tool for MLRP project development in Kaweah and Tule subbasins. Authors explicitly acknowledge weights have not yet been independently tested on real MLRP cases and note the tool is prospective (pre-implementation) rather than retrospective (post-implementation verification).
records.key_finding: A fuzzy logic multi-criteria scoring toolkit combining six suitability indices — including applied water rate, recharge potential, subsidence risk, and environmental health — can be operationalized as an interactive web tool for MLRP project siting in California subbasins, directly applicable to GAP's project evaluation and benefit attribution functions.
records.direct_quotes:
"Suitability values are calculated by combining different existing geospatial datasets that have been standardized to range from 0 (highly unsuitable) to 1 (highly suitable) for repurposing. The datasets are scaled and combined using fuzzy functions consistent with frequency distribution of the attribute." (Methods, Section 3.1, p. 4)

"Fuzzy logic was selected as it provides a flexible framework for defining suitability values along a spectrum, rather than relying on binary classifications... this methodology facilitates the translation of local stakeholder insights into the data standardization process, allowing for a continuous representation of suitability rather than forcing binary classifications." (Methods, Section 3.3, p. 7)
records.accounting_gap: Weights for the six suitability indices have not been independently tested on real MLRP project cases and may need adjustment after empirical testing. Tool addresses prospective siting and prioritization, not post-implementation benefit verification — the gap between which parcels to target and whether targeted parcels actually delivered projected benefits remains unaddressed. Water savings estimates use applied water rate as a proxy rather than direct ET measurement or metered pump data.
records.notes:
One of the only peer-reviewed paper explicitly built for and applied within MLRP.

Present six suitability indices through R Shiny, but used for planning and siting purposes pre-grant.

Tule and Kaweah are both active MLRP block grantees. Medellín-Azuara and Harmon (UC Merced) are central figures in the California agricultural water research community.

records.citation: Pace, C., Fencl, A., Baehner, L., Lukacs, H., Cushing, L.J., Morello-Frosch, R. (2022). The Drinking Water Tool: A Community-Driven Data Visualization Tool for Policy Implementation. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 19(3), 1419. DOI: 10.3390/ijerph19031419
records.geography: California (statewide; Central Valley/Central Coast focus)
records.analysis_method: The Community Water Center (CWC), an environmental justice organization, led development of the Drinking Water Tool (DWT) as part of the Water Equity Science Shop (WESS), a partnership combining community-based participatory research with the European Science Shop model. A stakeholder advisory committee shaped the tool before launch; 1.5 years later, WESS researchers evaluated the process through semi-structured interviews coded into three themes (engagement, policy impact, perception of community-led data).
records.key_finding: The engagement process itself, not just the resulting tool, was what stakeholders credited with improving interagency coordination and advancing policy conversations.
records.direct_quotes: "A large part of the power of [the Drinking Water Tool] was the conversation that developed through the stakeholder engagement process" ... "community engagement gets folks talking and advances the conversation on water justice." (Results)
records.learnings: A specific, traceable feedback loop worked: informal internal staff feedback (not the formal evaluation interviews) drove the shift to a two-portal design and refined the Spanish-language translation — ongoing informal input outperformed the one-time consultation. Failure point: the tool's finalization timeline did not align with the local Groundwater Sustainability Plan timeline, limiting its policy influence, and some agencies built parallel tools instead of adopting shared data layers.
records.community_selection: 15 stakeholders, purposively sampled and stratified by sector (government, academic, non-profit); eligible if affiliated with tool development, had attended a stakeholder webinar, or held subject-matter expertise. Interviews ran 40-60 minutes by video call. No compensation reported.
records.notes:
Compensation for interviewees not reported. Closest direct analog to the Groundwater Accounting Platform (GAP) of any paper in this review.

Question arose around who "owns" the tool. Researchers and interviewees trusted the Water Center but state agencies and GSA were reluctant to use a tool they didn't build.

records.citation: Pakparvar, M., Rezaei, M., Gabriels, D., Kowsar, S.A., Mossavi, S.A., & Cornelis, W. (2017). Assessment of groundwater recharge from a floodwater spreading system in an arid environment using water-budget and groundwater-level fluctuation methods. Hydrological Sciences Journal, 62(1), 147-164.
records.geography: Gareh Bygone Plain, Kowsar Station, Fars Province, southern Iran — arid desert environment (211mm mean annual precipitation); Bisheh Zard aquifer (7,600 ha); eight floodwater spreading (FWS) systems totaling 2,033 ha; 30-year dataset 1983-2012
records.accounting_method: (1) Weir-based water budget: diverted floodwater volumes measured at broad-crested weirs at each FWS system entry and exit point (since 2002); pre-2002 peak flows calculated using Manning's equation with slope-area method from channel cross-sections; retained volume (input minus output measured at tail drain weirs) = maximum possible recharge from floodwater spreading. (2) Water table fluctuation method: six observation wells (OW1-OW6) monitored monthly 1993-2012 by Fars Regional Water Organization; recharge estimated as ΔGW × Sy where Sy (specific yield) derived from laboratory measurements of soil samples from field investigations; temporal distribution of recharge assessed from monthly water level hydrographs before and after identified flood events. (3) Additionality partitioning: WAVES 1D soil-vegetation-atmosphere transfer model run with measured climate data for four soil-vegetation combinations to separate rainfall-induced recharge from floodwater spreading-induced recharge; artificial recharge proportion estimated as ratio of WTF-based recharge to total recharge from all sources.
records.data_sources: Broad-crested weirs at all FWS system diversion and outlet points; standard hydrometric station upstream of diversion dam (lymnograph with rating curve since 2002); six observation wells (monthly monitoring 1993-2012, resolution 0.01m); Gareh Bygone weather station (1996-2012); Baba Arab climatological station (1992-1996); WAVES soil-vegetation-atmosphere transfer model; soil laboratory analysis for specific yield estimation.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program. The Kowsar Station FWS system is an operational flood recharge program established in 1983 for desertification control and agricultural groundwater supply. However, accounting for what proportion of total recharge is attributable to floodwater spreading versus natural rainfall was a primary research question — no formal crediting mechanism for the recharge contribution exists.
records.key_finding: Floodwater spreading contributed 57-61% of total groundwater recharge in the Bisheh Zard aquifer during 2010-11, estimated by combining weir-measured diversion volumes with water table fluctuation recharge calculations — providing an operational proof-of-concept for attributing a specific fraction of aquifer recharge to deliberate flood diversion operations using only flow measurement and groundwater level monitoring.
records.direct_quotes:
"The volume of floodwater diverted to the FWS systems from January 1983 to November 2002 has been estimated and reported... Since November 2002, there have been two types of flow measurements in the FWS systems in the study area. First, peak flow was recorded at the hydrometric station, and second, diverted flow inside the FWS systems was measured by broad-crested weirs." (Methods, Section 2.2, p. 148)

"The flow rate of water entering and leaving the FWS systems in the study area is measured similarly. Therefore, the volume of water that is retained in the individual FWS systems and in the entire project is calculated in every event." (Methods, Section 2.2, p. 149)
records.accounting_gap: Specific yield — the conversion factor between observed water table rise and estimated recharge volume — is estimated from laboratory soil samples and is a primary source of uncertainty in the WTF method. Monthly monitoring frequency of observation wells is insufficient to capture rapid water table responses to short-duration flood events, potentially missing or underestimating recharge from quick-response floods. Long-term decline in some groundwater levels despite active recharge demonstrates that additionality assessment must account for concurrent pumping demand, not just supply.
records.notes:
Most analogous to California Kings River and San Joaquin Valley flood-MAR operations.

The weir + water table fluctuation dual method is operationally practical and directly applicable to existing California flood diversion infrastructure, but still reliant on an accurate specific yeild estimate.

30-year dataset is the longest operational flood recharge record reviewed.

records.citation: Pauloo, R.A., Escriva-Bou, A., Dahlke, H., Fencl, A., Guillon, H., & Fogg, G.E. (2020). Domestic well vulnerability to drought duration and unsustainable groundwater management in California's Central Valley. Environmental Research Letters, 15(4), 044010.
records.geography: California Central Valley, USA (67,011 domestic wells, focus on southeastern CV subbasins)
records.accounting_method:
(1) Well failure classification: wells classified as failing when kriging-interpolated seasonal groundwater levels fall at or below estimated pump intake depth; pump intake depth estimated as mean of static water level at completion and top of screened interval from 943,469 well completion reports.
(2) Drought scenario simulation: groundwater level change from 2012–2016 drought scaled by 0.25–1.0 to simulate 5–8 year extended drought durations; cumulative well failures projected using the calibrated spatial model.
(3) Management regime projection: three SGMA-aligned scenarios (strict sustainability, glide path, business as usual) projected to 2040 using ordinary kriging of 1998–2017 seasonal groundwater levels at 5×5 km raster resolution; well failures estimated for each regime.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No operational crediting program. Model designed as a policy planning tool to evaluate SGMA management regime impacts on domestic well failure. Authors explicitly state the model could be used by water resources managers and policymakers to evaluate management strategies.
records.key_finding: Under business-as-usual groundwater management, 5,966–10,466 additional domestic well failures are projected by 2040 in the Central Valley; strict SGMA sustainability reduces this to 1,516–2,513. Demonstrating that a quantitative well failure model can directly translate groundwater management regime choices into measurable DAC impacts.
records.direct_quotes:
"Wells are classified as vulnerable to well failure when the groundwater level in a well falls within 3 m of the pump intake... we estimate the minimum separation distance required to avoid decreases in well function as 3 m." (Methods, Section 3.2)

"In the 'intervening wet winter' scenario, groundwater levels are allowed to recover during 2017, and well failure slightly abates: 498 and 738 fewer wells fail in the 6 and 8 year drought scenarios, indicating that an increase in median groundwater level of only a few meters across the Central Valley can prevent hundreds of domestic well failures during extended drought." (Results, Section 4.2)
records.accounting_gap: Reported well failure data under-counts actual failures due to voluntary reporting. Model calibration constrained by incomplete ground truth. Pump intake depth must be imputed for most wells due to missing WCR data. Model does not account for well owners who deepen wells in response to water table decline, which underestimates actual vulnerability.
records.notes:
Potential for DAC Co-benefits of recharge, without explicity mentioning. Well failure accounting.

The model gives a framework for translating a specific volume of recharge into an estimated number of domestic well failures prevented.

The 3m pump-intake threshold for vulnerable wells could apply to GAP benefit attribution for recharge projects near domestic wells.

records.citation: Perrone, D., Rohde, M.M., Hammond Wagner, C., Anderson, R., Arthur, S., Atume, N., Brown, M., Esaki-Kua, L., Gonzalez Fernandez, M., Garvey, K.A., Heidel, K., Jones, W.D., Khosrowshahi Asl, S., Munill, C., Nelson, R., Ortiz-Partida, J.P., Remson, E.J. (2023). Stakeholder integration predicts better outcomes from groundwater sustainability policy. Nature Communications, 14, 3793. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-023-39363-y
records.geography: California, statewide (108 Sustainability Plans under SGMA)
records.analysis_method: Read and coded 162,943 pages across 108 GSPs to score how well each plan integrates three stakeholder groups (agriculture, domestic, environment) across four components — engage, describe, analyze, act — producing an aggregate 0-8 integration score per group per plan. Separately, built a geospatial layer identifying which domestic wells, agricultural wells, and groundwater-dependent ecosystems fall within ~2.4 km of a representative monitoring well ("covered") and whether that well's minimum threshold sits above the stakeholder's groundwater access depth ("protected"). Statistically tested whether integration scores predict coverage/protection using Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn, t-tests, ANOVA, and OLS regression, and repeated the analysis for two economically vulnerable subgroups (small farms, disadvantaged communities).
records.key_finding: Integration is not decorative — when a plan meaningfully integrates the domestic or environment stakeholder group, that group is measurably more protected (domestic: +4.3% well protection per integration point, p ≤ 0.01; environment: +3.0% ecosystem protection per point, p ≤ 0.05), but agricultural stakeholders show no such relationship because they already hold formal governance authority through irrigation/reclamation districts on GSA boards — engagement matters most for groups that lack a seat by default.
records.direct_quotes:
"...we show that: (1) 91% of Sustainability Plans did not integrate stakeholders comprehensively and (2) Sustainability Plans do not protect 60% of agricultural wells, 63% of domestic wells, and 91% of ecosystems." (Results)

"...found domestic wells within disadvantaged communities to be significantly less protected than domestic wells outside these communities (p ≤ 0.001)." (Results)
records.learnings: "Coverage" (does a monitoring well exist near a stakeholder at all) and "protection" (is the threshold at that well actually protective) are two separable, quantifiable accounting failures, and the paper's methodology — buffering wells/ecosystems around representative monitoring wells and comparing access depth to minimum threshold — is a directly reusable spatial method GAP could adapt to flag un-covered or under-protected wells and habitat. Disadvantaged communities had integration scores too uniformly low to statistically test the integration-protection relationship at all — an absence of variation that is itself a finding about current GSP practice.
records.community_selection: Not a human-subjects study — the "stakeholders" are groundwater wells and ecosystems identified from GSP text and geospatial well-completion/land-use records, not interviewed people. Five to seven trained coders scored each GSP against a shared rubric across three coding rounds (draft 2022 GSPs, final 2022 GSPs, and a re-coding pass); intercoder reliability for the engage component was checked with two independent coders (Cohen's kappa > 0.7).
records.notes:
Largest-scale, most rigorous quantitative evidence in the review that stakeholder engagement in SGMA documents correlates with a measurable protection outcome, not just participation.

Methodologically close to a ready-made accounting layer for GAP: the coverage/protection buffer method could be run basin-by-basin as a standing indicator, and the engage/describe/analyze/act rubric could be adapted to score a GSP's Community Considerations content specifically.

Does not evaluate ISW or MLRP directly, but the coverage/protection method is directly portable to either.

records.citation: Racz, A.J., Fisher, A.T., Schmidt, C.M., Lockwood, B.S., & Los Huertos, M. (2011). Spatial and temporal infiltration dynamics during managed aquifer recharge. Groundwater, 50(4), 562–570.
records.geography: Harkins Slough MAR pond, Pajaro Valley, central coastal California, USA (3-ha infiltration basin, Holocene alluvial and fluvial deposits, 15-20m depth to water table)
records.accounting_method:
(1) Whole-pond water budget mass balance: net infiltration I = D + P - E - ΔV, where D = diversions from Harkins Slough measured hourly by flow meter; P = precipitation measured by tipping bucket gauge; E = evaporation calculated hourly from CIMIS station PET; ΔV = change in pond storage calculated every 15 minutes from autonomous pressure gauge in stilling well combined with pond digital elevation model. Values normalized by wetted area to derive specific infiltration rate (m/d).
(2) Point-specific heat tracer method: subsurface temperature recorded at 15-minute intervals at 20, 40, and 80 cm depths below pond sediment interface at eight piezometer locations; amplitude reduction and phase shift of diurnal temperature signal between sensor pairs solved for daily fluid infiltration rate using one-dimensional conservation-of-heat equation (Hatch et al. 2006).
records.data_sources: Harkins Slough diversion flow meter (hourly); CIMIS Watsonville West Station 209 (PET, precipitation verification); autonomous pressure gauge and pond DEM (pond stage and volume); 8 PVC piezometers with thermal and pressure loggers (15-30 min intervals); Beckman Coulter laser diffraction particle size analyzer (soil texture); survey benchmarks referenced to mean sea level.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program. Study conducted by Pajaro Valley Water Management Agency, which is permitted to divert up to 2.5 million m3 of surface runoff annually. Recovery wells adjacent to the pond withdraw shallow groundwater blended with other supplies for agricultural distribution. No SGMA-era accounting or crediting framework described.
records.key_finding: Infiltration is an upper bound on aquifer recharge, not recharge itself, because water trapped in the vadose zone during early-season operations can be returned to the atmosphere by ET; whole-pond mass balance consistently exceeded point-specific heat tracer rates, confirming spatial heterogeneity and measurement scale effects that propagate as uncertainty into any recharge credit claimed.
records.direct_quotes:
"Not all of the water infiltrated during MAR becomes recharge. Some infiltration becomes trapped in the vadose zone as soil water, particularly infiltration that occurs near the start of the MAR operation season, and can be returned to the atmosphere by evaporation and transpiration." (Methods, p. 2)

"Whole-pond infiltration, normalized for wetted area, rose rapidly to more than 1.0 m/d at the start of MAR operations (increasing as pond stage rose), was sustained at high rates for the next 40 d, and then decreased to less than 0.1 m/d by the end of the recharge season." (Results, p. 5)
records.accounting_gap: The vadose zone represents an unquantified loss between measured infiltration and confirmed aquifer recharge — the paper establishes this gap exists but does not provide a method for quantifying the vadose zone storage fraction at a given site. Point-specific measurements cannot be spatially extrapolated to the whole pond without accounting for the shifting spatial distribution of infiltration hot spots that the paper documents. There is no method described for distinguishing credited MAR recharge from background natural recharge occurring simultaneously.
records.notes:
The standard pond-level water budget measures infiltration, not aquifer recharge.

GAP must be clear about which quantity it is crediting infiltration or confirmed recharge to aquifer. Uncertainty between these two values is site-specific and unresolved by this paper alone.

California site (Pajaro Valley)

records.citation: Rohde, M.M., Stella, J.C., Singer, M.B., Roberts, D.A., Caylor, K.K., & Albano, C.M. (2024). Establishing ecological thresholds and targets for groundwater management. Nature Water.
records.geography: California, USA (statewide: 246,017 GDE vegetation polygons)
records.accounting_method:
(1) Annual dry-season NDVI (1985–2022) extracted for 246,017 NCCAG GDE polygons and standardized to Z scores (ZNDVI) by subtracting each polygon's 38-year mean and dividing by its standard deviation; DTG from CASGEM wells paired to 3,113 polygons within 250m and standardized to ZDTG using the same approach.
(2) For 289 polygons with a significant negative ZNDVI–ZDTG regression (slope <0, p ≤ 0.05), the ZDTG value at ZNDVI = -1 was interpolated as the local adverse impact threshold, yielding a statewide conservative management threshold of ZDTG = 1.3 (~4.0m DTG at the 25th percentile).
(3) For the 98.7% of GDE polygons lacking well data, the percentage of drought years where ZNDVI ≥ 0 was calculated for each polygon to map potential groundwater-buffered drought refugia statewide.
records.data_sources: TNC GDE Pulse v2.1 tool (Landsat-derived NDVI for NCCAG polygons, 1985–2022); California CASGEM groundwater monitoring wells; Audubon Kern River Preserve shallow monitoring network; USGS 1/3 arcsecond DEM; TNC Plant Rooting Depth Database; USDA drought monitor standardized precipitation index.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program. Framework designed for GSA and conservation practitioners for SGMA GSP impact assessments and Public Trust Doctrine evaluations. Authors recommend adaptive management approach with locally robust groundwater-level data.
records.key_finding: Z score standardization (ZDTG threshold ~1.3–1.8, corresponding to ~4.0m DTG) provides a scalable, reproducible threshold metric for identifying groundwater levels that trigger adverse GDE impacts which could enable ecosystem accounting in GSPs without requiring dense local monitoring networks.
records.direct_quotes:
"Z scores were calculated for each annual observation at each vegetation polygon by subtracting the average annual dry-season NDVI observation by the site-specific mean and then dividing by the standard deviation, resulting in 9,343,646 ZNDVI data points across California... For each of the 289 vegetation polygons with a significant negative slope, we used a threshold of ZNDVI = −1 to interpolate the corresponding ZDTG value, where larger positive ZDTG scores correspond with deeper groundwater anomalies." (Methods, p. 10)

"Groundwater-dependent vegetation with a higher percentage of positive ZNDVI values during drought years are more likely to be drought refugia than vegetation with a lower percentage of positive ZNDVI values." (Results, p. 7)
records.accounting_gap: Groundwater data available for only 1.3% of mapped GDE vegetation polygons statewide. Sparse monitoring severely limits threshold-based accounting at scale. Static polygon boundaries do not capture dynamic land cover changes. Chronic community-level responses (species shifts, recruitment decline) not captured by NDVI approach.

records.citation: Sauermilch, W., Irving, J., Reams, M., Guo, C., Cormier, S., Richmond-Bryant, J. (2024). Empowering Citizens Through the Development and Deployment of a Community-Based Environmental Health Reporting Tool. Environmental Justice. DOI: 10.1089/env.2024.0013
records.geography: Colfax, Louisiana (rural, low-technology-access community); not California
records.analysis_method: Researchers developed community-specific reporting booklets translating air-pollution monitoring data for residents near a hazardous waste facility, refined over seven distribution rounds with input from a Community Engagement Advisory Committee, then evaluated the booklets against Universal Design for Learning criteria (multiple means of representation, engagement, and action/expression) rather than through a formal reader survey.
records.key_finding: The booklets were cited in a regulatory permit decision and used in resident advocacy and legal claims — direct evidence that a well-translated data product can influence agency decisions, not just inform residents.
records.direct_quotes: "Listening attentively to residents' personal narratives, taking time for each conversation so that residents do not feel rushed, and working diligently in hot, humid weather all helped to earn the trust of community members." (Methods)
records.learnings: A formal survey attempt failed outright due to insufficient responses in this small community, so the authors relied on informal meeting observation instead — a caution that a survey instrument will not necessarily work in every community context. Authors explicitly warn a tool built for one community's needs may not transfer to another.
records.community_selection: All community residents were eligible; researchers specifically targeted households not represented at community meetings via door-to-door visits, home visits during equipment maintenance, and meeting distribution. No monetary compensation, but the booklets were designed for accessibility — a 7th-grade reading level, a color-coded flowchart, and results labeled with residents' own names (cleared by the university's ethics review board) so neighbors had a familiar frame of reference.
records.notes:
No California context. Strongest example in the review of trust built through time and physical presence rather than formal instruments.

Applied a Universal Design for Learning (UDL) framework.

Formal survey failed for the small community.

records.citation: Sorgen, J., Nelson, P., Butsic, V., LaRosa, S., Gaughen, S., Crosby, E., Geary, R., & Sowerwine, J. (2025). Unchecking the box: Overcoming barriers to meaningful consultation. Environmental Science & Policy, 169, 104085. DOI: 10.1016/j.envsci.2025.104085
records.geography: California, statewide (Tribal ancestral lands, cannabis-permitting context); not SGMA-specific
records.analysis_method: Researchers conducted 28 semi-structured interviews with 33 Tribal representatives and 20 interviews with 39 agency representatives (plus archaeologists, cultivators, and academics) about government-to-government Tribal consultation under California's cannabis-permitting laws, guided throughout by a paid seven-member Tribal advisory committee that shaped the study design, questions, and analysis; interview data were coded using a grounded-theory approach to derive five recurring barrier categories.
records.key_finding: The study identifies five recurring barrier categories to meaningful consultation — agency discretion, weak enforcement, prioritization of Western knowledge, knowledge/data sovereignty, and capacity — and argues the first two are structural root causes that make the others, including data sovereignty, consequential in practice.
records.direct_quotes: "It is the authority and capacity to approve and shape a project that ultimately makes consultation meaningful." (Discussion)
records.learnings: The paper distinguishes "structural" barriers (rooted in power asymmetry, like agency discretion and weak enforcement) from "soft" barriers (cultural differences, knowledge gaps, poor relationships), arguing soft barriers are how dysfunction is experienced day-to-day but structural barriers are what actually needs fixing — a useful frame for diagnosing whether a specific Tribal engagement problem needs a relational fix or a genuine authority-sharing fix.
records.community_selection: Tribal representatives were reached through the Native American Heritage Commission's contact list and the advisory team's professional networks; agency representatives were reached through the advisory team's connections to county and state planning departments; advisory committee members and Tribal interviewees were explicitly paid as expert consultants, not treated as unpaid human subjects, and the research protocol passed both university ethics review and separate Tribal oversight through the California Rural Indian Health Board.
records.notes:
Government-to-government Tribal consultation under different legal authority (AB 52/CEQA, cannabis permitting) than SGMA.

Its "knowledge/data sovereignty" barrier category is the clearest documented articulation yet of why a Tribe's data needs may not be resolvable the same way disadvantaged-community data needs are.

records.citation: Walker, D., Parkin, G., Schmitter, P., Gowing, J., Tilahun, S.A., Haile, A.T., & Yimam, A.Y. (2018). Insights from a multi-method recharge estimation comparison study. Groundwater, 57(2), 245–258.
records.geography: Dangila woreda, Amhara Region, northwest Ethiopia (900 km2; shallow aquifer in weathered basalt regolith; moist subtropical climate, 1,541 mm mean annual precipitation)
records.accounting_method:
(1) Nine recharge estimation methods applied with 17 variations: empirical rainfall-recharge relationship from 102 Ethiopian studies; streamflow hydrograph methods (3 variations: Meyboom recession, Rorabaugh, Rutledge automated digital filter); soil moisture balance (2 variations: simple and FAO-56 Penman-Monteith ET); basin water balance (3 variations with and without interflow); chloride mass balance from 31 groundwater samples vs. 3 rainfall samples; water table fluctuation using bi-daily groundwater level measurements in 25 hand-dug wells combined with specific yield estimates; rainfall infiltration breakthrough from hydrograph response timing; physically based modeling (MIKE SHE); and 3 published large-scale mapping studies.
(2) Critical assessment framework: each result evaluated against what type of recharge it represents (actual, potential, or minimum), spatial and temporal scale of measurement, and degree to which method assumptions are satisfied at the site.
records.data_sources: NMA weather station Dangila (1987-2017, rainfall and temperature); Amen and Kilti river flow gauging stations (1988/1997-2014); community-based monitoring network (25 hand-dug wells bi-daily, river stage twice-daily, daily rainfall 2014-2017); 31 groundwater samples and 3 rainfall samples for chloride analysis (Dionex ion chromatography); WHYMAP, Altchenko & Villholth (2015), and Ayenew et al. (2008) for large-scale model comparison; MIKE SHE physically based model.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program. Study is a methodological comparison designed to improve recharge estimation practice. Authors explicitly recommend multi-method approaches and critical assessment of what each method measures before reporting results.
records.key_finding: Nine methods applied to the same site produced recharge estimates ranging from 45 to 814 mm/year — an 18-fold range — which narrowed to 280-430 mm/year after critical assessment of what each method actually measures; method choice alone can dominate the recharge estimate, and most widely used methods were not calibrated against observed data, making uncertainty characterization impossible without multi-method comparison.
records.direct_quotes:
"Nine separate groundwater recharge estimation methods, with a total of 17 variations, were applied at a shallow aquifer in northwest Ethiopia... These gave a wide range of recharge values from 45 to 814 mm/a. Critical assessment indicated that the results depended on what the recharge represents (actual, potential, minimum recharge or change in aquifer storage), and spatial and temporal scales, as well as uncertainties from application of each method." (Abstract, p. 1)

"Only one method involved calibration to observations; most widely used recharge methods did not, which the authors identify as a major uncertainty issue." (Results, Consensus Recharge Estimate section, p. 255)
records.accounting_gap: Method selection in practice is driven by data availability rather than methodological suitability, meaning that the method used by a GSA is often not the best method for its specific hydrogeological conditions. Results are only comparable across sites when the type of recharge being estimated (actual vs. potential vs. minimum) is explicitly stated — which most published studies and operational programs do not do. Calibration against independent observations is rare, leaving uncertainty uncharacterized for most real-world applications.
records.notes:
Set in Ethiopia but finding applicable to CA GSAs.

18-fold range in estimates is evidence for why GAP needs a standardized accounting methodology.

Cite in methods document when discussing why recharge volume uncertainty is a fundamental challenge for crediting programs.

records.citation: Whittemore, D.O., Butler, J.J., Bohling, G.C., & Wilson, B.B. (2023). Are we saving water? Simple methods for assessing the effectiveness of groundwater conservation measures. Agricultural Water Management, 287, 108408.
records.geography: Kansas High Plains (Ogallala) Aquifer, USA — SD-6 LEMA (256 km²), Wichita County GMD1 (county scale), and five Groundwater Management Districts (GMD1-5; several thousand to over 20,000 km²)
records.accounting_method: (1) Precipitation-pumping regression for conservation verification: annual irrigation groundwater use per irrigated area plotted against January-September radar precipitation for pre-conservation and conservation periods; a downward shift in the regression line intercept between periods, confirmed by F-tests comparing parallel-slopes versus single-line reference models, indicates true water conservation independent of climate variability. (2) Conservation component decomposition: total water use reduction separated into (a) efficiency improvement (regression of pumping per irrigated area vs. precipitation) and (b) irrigated area reduction (difference between per-area and total pumping regressions). The parallel-slopes model intercept difference quantifies the climate-adjusted conservation effect in cm per irrigated area or total volume.
records.data_sources: NOAA AHPS multi-sensor radar precipitation (~4x4 km resolution, 2005-present); WIMAS metered annual pumping records for all permitted wells (~98% of wells have totalizing flowmeters); irrigated area from WIMAS self-reports and Deines et al. (2019) satellite-derived AIM; F-test statistical framework (Draper and Smith, 1981) for significance of regression model differences.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: Documented operational programs evaluated. The SD-6 LEMA (est. 2013, goal: 20% pumping reduction), GMD4 district-wide LEMA (est. 2018, variable township goals), Wichita County Water Conservation Areas (est. 2017) and county LEMA (est. 2021), and GMD1 four-county proposed LEMA. All operate under Kansas K.S.A. 82a-1041 with mandatory metered reporting, enforceable allocations, and GMD/KDA-DWR regulatory oversight. GMD4 LEMA showed minimal conservation effect in first four years due to legal challenges delaying irrigator participation.
records.key_finding: Linear regression of radar precipitation against metered annual pumping detects statistically significant water savings of 25-27% in SD-6 and 23-38% in Wichita County attributable to LEMA and WCA programs — a simple, scalable verification method requiring only precipitation data and metered pump records that could serve as a low-cost demand management accounting tool for GSAs with equivalent data infrastructure.
records.direct_quotes:
"Relationships between pumping and precipitation help provide an answer, as precipitation explains most of the variation in annual irrigation water use for aquifers in semi-arid to sub-humid climates when surface water supplies are limited." (Abstract, p. 1)

"These relationships are dependent on high-quality precipitation and groundwater use data. High-quality precipitation data are often available, but reliable groundwater use data are not... Kansas is an outlier in this regard as it has some of the best water use data for aquifers in the US." (Conclusions, p. 8)

records.geography: Little Shasta River (northern California, Shasta/Klamath basin, spring-influenced); lower Cosumnes River (central California, Central Valley, floodplain groundwater-influenced)
records.accounting_method:
(1) CEFF Sections A and B applied to two groundwater-influenced river systems. Section A: download predicted natural ranges of functional flow metrics (fall pulse flow, wet-season baseflow, peak flows, spring recession, dry-season baseflow) from the California Natural Flows database, modeled from reference gages. Section B: evaluate whether groundwater contributions — discrete spring volumes, shallow perched aquifer inputs, channel incision effects on floodplain connectivity — require revision of the natural flow metric ranges. Groundwater influence assessed via existing spring discharge measurements, subsurface stratigraphy, and documented groundwater-surface water interaction studies.
(2) Water quality co-benefit assessment: review of existing studies on temperature, nutrient, and contaminant concentrations at each site to determine whether baseflow quality (cool temperature, high nutrients from springs, limited contaminants) modifies dry-season flow target recommendations.
records.data_sources: California Natural Flows database (functional flow metrics from hydrologic models calibrated to reference gages); Shasta Watermaster historical spring discharge records (early 20th century); USGS gage 11516900 (Little Shasta headwaters, inactive) and 11517000 (Shasta River mainstem); DWR NCCAG GDE polygons; existing published studies on channel morphology, groundwater elevation, and salmon habitat at each site; Kleinschmidt Associates (2008) lower Cosumnes biological data.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program. CEFF is a structured planning framework developed by the California Water Quality Monitoring Council for setting environmental flow standards. Paper demonstrates CEFF's application to groundwater-influenced streams. Results provide ecological flow needs for watershed stakeholders to use in developing environmental flow recommendations under CEFF Section C.
records.key_finding: CEFF's functional flows approach can explicitly incorporate groundwater contributions to dry-season baseflow, spring sources, and water quality into ecological flow target-setting, but only where groundwater influence on surface flow is well-characterized by existing data; at sites with poorly characterized groundwater-surface water interactions, CEFF Section B revisions cannot be made defensibly.
records.direct_quotes:
"We assessed the potential for contributions of groundwater to enhance surface flows at each study site, especially during the dry season when runoff from precipitation is limited or lacking and flows are often sustained by groundwater inputs. We evaluated existing studies and knowledge of known groundwater inputs, such as discrete spring volumes, and determined whether these contributions should be considered in our estimates of the natural range of dry season baseflow magnitude or other functional flow components." (Methods, Section 2.1, p. 3)

"Reduced floodplain connectivity can limit functions such as groundwater recharge that support gaining stream conditions and extended riparian soil moisture for GDEs, and highly incised channels can cause groundwater levels to fall below riparian vegetation rooting depths, resulting in the loss of riparian vegetation and habitat." (Methods, Section 2.1, p. 4)
records.accounting_gap: CEFF does not provide a quantitative method for measuring groundwater contributions to streamflow. Instead, it synthesizes existing knowledge rather than generating new measurements. Historical flow data prior to agricultural development and spring diversions are unavailable at most sites, making 'natural' baseflow targets inherently uncertain. Channel incision effects on groundwater-surface water connectivity are described qualitatively, not quantified. The framework cannot be applied defensibly where groundwater-surface water interactions are poorly characterized.
records.notes:
Most relevant to 7. ecological co-benefits than pure ISW accounting: CEFF translates groundwater contributions into ecological flow targets rather than quantifying depletion volumes.

Relevance to GAP is primarily for incorporating environmental flow considerations into ISW accounting: when a recharge project raises baseflow, CEFF provides a framework for attributing that benefit to specific ecological outcomes.

Could be used in tandem with Rohde et al. (2024) to attribute ecological co-benefits of recharge projects ot to terrestrial GDE and aquatic habitat in ISW.

records.geography: Archetypal steady-state numerical model of the groundwater system around Nanaimo, Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada; three sub-domains (7.6 km² high density to 81.6 km² low density) selected along a natural east-west drainage density gradient
records.accounting_method: Evaluates five geometric "depletion apportionment equations" that distribute analytically-estimated streamflow depletion across a stream network with multiple reaches: (1) Thiessen polygon (area-based), (2) inverse distance, (3) inverse distance squared, and two new methods introduced in this paper — (4) web and (5) web squared — which weight depletion using distance to a series of equally spaced (5 m) points along the entire length of each stream reach rather than just the single closest point
records.data_sources: Steady-state MODFLOW-2005 finite-difference model across three drainage-density sub-domains; stream network geometry from the Canadian National Hydro Network; Canada digital elevation model for topographic relief sensitivity tests; 50–62 synthetic pumping wells per domain (pumped one-at-a-time at 1,000 m³/d, or 5,000 m³/d in recharge-relief tests); five recharge rates tested (0.01–1.0 m/yr)
records.formal_program_or_crediting: None directly — framed as groundwork toward operational management tools. Cites the Michigan Water Withdrawal Assessment Tool (Reeves et al., 2009) as the only existing operational precedent for embedding a depletion apportionment equation into a permitting tool
records.key_finding: The new "web squared" method consistently best matched MODFLOW results across all conditions tested — KGE of 0.543 (high density), 0.626 (medium density), and 0.765 (low density) under flat, no-recharge conditions, followed by inverse distance squared. Performance of all five equations declined as drainage density, topographic relief, and recharge rate increased, and as stream reach length shortened (<0.1 km reaches performed worst).
records.direct_quotes: "Web squared, a new method introduced here which explicitly considers stream network geometry, performs the best across a range of drainage density, topographic, and groundwater recharge scenarios, followed by the inverse distance squared method." (Section 5, Synthesis and Conclusions, p. 5484)
records.accounting_gap: All five apportionment equations showed a negative bias — systematically underestimating depletion — ranging from −0.2% (Thiessen polygon, flat low-density domain) to −72.2% (inverse distance, flat high-density domain), the opposite of the conservative (over-)estimation preferred for avoiding water over-allocation. Error in web squared specifically was fairly evenly split — 37–71% correlation, 23–43% variability, 6–21% bias — vs. Thiessen polygon, where 85–100% of error was correlation-driven. Tested only under steady-state conditions; explicitly flagged as needing extension to transient pumping and combination with an analytical depletion model to be operational (which the authors note they were pursuing in "ongoing research" — this became the 2019 paper). Not tested for short (<0.1 km) reaches, near coastlines/variable-density flow, or streams that dry seasonally.
records.notes: Method is implemented in the open-source R package, streamDepletr
