records.citation: Zipper, S.C., Gleeson, T., Kerr, B., Howard, J.K., Rohde, M.M., Carah, J., & Zimmerman, J. (2019). Rapid and accurate estimates of streamflow depletion caused by groundwater pumping using analytical depletion functions. Water Resources Research, 55(7), 5807–5829. https://doi.org/10.1029/2018WR024403
records.geography: Navarro River Watershed, California, USA (archetypal numerical model domain); method is broadly applicable to real-world stream networks
records.accounting_method:
(1) Analytical depletion function (ADF) construction: three sequential components applied to each well. Step 1 (stream proximity criteria): identify which stream segments may be affected using one of five criteria including the best-performing 'expanding' criterion, which uses the analytical model to calculate the maximum distance with depletion potential exceeding 1% at each time step. Step 2 (depletion apportionment equation): distribute total depletion among affected segments; the best-performing 'web squared' equation weights depletion by stream network geometry and segment length. Step 3 (analytical streamflow depletion model): estimate volumetric depletion rate in each segment using the Hunt (1999) model, which includes streambed resistance to flow via a streambed conductance parameter.
(2) Performance evaluation: 50 ADFs compared to a calibrated MODFLOW numerical model using Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) and mean absolute error (MAE) across transient conditions.
(3) Depletion potential output: Qd,i = fi * (Qa,i / Qw) for each stream segment i, where fi is the apportioned fraction and Qa,i is the analytical depletion rate.
records.data_sources: Calibrated MODFLOW numerical model of the Navarro River Watershed (California); stream network delineated from 10m National Elevation Dataset; five stream proximity criteria tested computationally; streamDepletr R package (Zipper, 2019) — open-source implementation of all 50 ADFs; Hunt (1999) analytical model for streambed conductance; Glover-Balmer (1954) and Hantush (1965) analytical models as comparison benchmarks.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program. Authors explicitly designed ADFs as decision support tools for locations without calibrated numerical models. Notes Michigan Water Withdrawal Assessment Tool (WWAT) as the only existing operational example integrating a streamflow depletion model into a permitting process. Open-source streamDepletr R package provided as a deployable implementation.
records.key_finding: The best-performing ADF combining expanding stream proximity criteria, web-squared depletion apportionment, and the Hunt analytical model correctly identifies the most-depleted stream segment for more than 70% of pumping wells with mean absolute error below 15% of predicted depletion — providing a scalable, open-source alternative to numerical modeling for well-level ISW screening in locations where MODFLOW models are unavailable.
records.direct_quotes:
"We define an analytical depletion function as the combination of three components: stream proximity criteria, which determine the stream segments impacted by a well; a depletion apportionment equation, which distributes depletion among impacted stream segments; and an analytical model to estimate streamflow depletion in each segment." (Methods, Section 2, p. 5809)

"Analytical depletion functions predict streamflow depletion more accurately than analytical models alone. The choice of a depletion apportionment equation has the largest impact on analytical depletion function performance and equations that consider stream network geometry perform best." (Abstract, p. 5807)
records.accounting_gap: ADFs perform best for wells within approximately 3 km of streams in relatively flat terrain; performance degrades for wells further from streams and in complex topography. The expanding stream proximity criteria require more computation than static criteria, posing practical barriers for large-scale deployment. ADF accuracy is still substantially lower than calibrated numerical models for complex multi-stream systems. Streambed conductance is difficult to measure at regional scale and is a primary source of ADF uncertainty.
records.notes:
Most directly actionable ISW paper for GAP's proposed ISW accounting.

streamDepletr R package is open-source and deployable without numerical modeling infrastructure.

The three-component ADF structure maps cleanly onto a scalable GSA-level screening tool. Study domain is Navarro River Watershed in California, making findings directly applicable to California aquifer settings.

Note Zipper (2018) is the predecessor methodological paper to Zipper (2022).

records.citation: Zipper, S.C., Farmer, W.H., Brookfield, A., Ajami, H., Reeves, H.W., Wardropper, C., Hammond, J.C., Gleeson, T., & Deines, J.M. (2022). Quantifying streamflow depletion from groundwater pumping: A practical review of past and emerging approaches for water management. Journal of the American Water Resources Association, 58(2), 282–310.
records.geography: Western United States (broadly applicable); examples from Colorado, Michigan, and San Pedro Basin, Arizona
records.accounting_method:
(1) Analytical models: estimate streamflow depletion from a single well using aquifer transmissivity, storativity, and distance to stream; the Glover-Balmer (1954) solution and the derived Streamflow Depletion Factor (SDF), which is the time for depletion to equal 28% of pumped volume, are the regulatory standard in Colorado and other prior appropriation states.
(2) Numerical models (gold standard): estimate depletion by differencing streamflow in paired simulations with and without pumping in MODFLOW or integrated hydrologic models; account for 3D aquifer heterogeneity, vadose zone dynamics, and phreatophytic ET simultaneously.
(3) Statistical models: identify depletion trends via regression of streamflow and pumping records but produce correlative rather than causative output, limiting use for attribution and mitigation decisions. Paper develops four decision criteria for model selection: suitability to local conditions, actionability, transparency, and reproducibility.
records.data_sources: Review-based — no primary datasets. Semi-structured conversations with five water managers spanning water planning, regulation, environmental consulting, and NGO roles. Web of Science and Google Scholar literature search. Forward and backward citation tracing.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program. Documents two operational examples: (1) Colorado's SDF-based regulatory framework for ISW depletion by wells near streams with senior rights holders; (2) Michigan's Water Withdrawal Assessment Tool (WWAT), which integrates an analytical model with a depletion apportionment equation to screen high-capacity well registrations statewide using risk-based depletion criteria — 3,400 registrations completed over 11 years.
records.key_finding: ISW depletion cannot be directly measured at regional scale, only estimated, and the choice between analytical, numerical, and statistical approaches should be governed by the management question being addressed (attribution vs. impacts vs. mitigation), not by default to one method; numerical models are the gold standard for impacts and mitigation but are infeasible for many resource-constrained GSAs.
records.direct_quotes:
"While streamflow depletion can be measured at the scale of an individual stream reach using intensive field measurements, it is not possible to measure streamflow depletion at the regional scale, nor resolve depletion in individual segments, using observational data alone." (Methods, p. 288)

"Analytical models are well-suited for rapid, screening-level assessments of potential impacts and implications of streamflow depletion, but they struggle with questions related to attribution and mitigation since they rarely include other processes that could affect streamflow. Numerical models are currently the gold standard for streamflow depletion estimation, but can be infeasible in many settings with limited resources." (Conclusions, p. 305)
records.accounting_gap: No consistent regulatory framework for ISW depletion exists across jurisdictions. GSAs make decisions on a case-by-case basis. Statistical approaches cannot establish causation, limiting their use for SGMA compliance. Analytical depletion functions offer improved accuracy over standalone analytical models but require additional testing. Uncertainty quantification is critical but rarely communicated to water managers alongside depletion estimates.
records.notes:
Great review and foundation for ISW cluster framing.

Analytical low data needs and cpu costs, assumed causation and best use for screening / impacts. Numerical high data and cpu costs, explicit caussatoni and best use for impacts / mititgation. Stats (ML, etc.) moderate data needs, low cpu, correlative only and best used for attribution screening and may not support SGMA compliance.

The SDF could be a defensible screening-level estimate with minimal data. Michigan WWAT an example of analytical model being turned into a decision support tool.

Estimating irrigation water use from remotely sensed evapotranspiration data: Accuracy and uncertainties at field, water right, and regional scales. Agricultural Water Management, 303, 109036.

records.accounting_method:
(1) Field-scale validation: OpenET ensemble mean precipitation deficit (ET minus effective precipitation, April-October growing season) compared against farmer-reported irrigation application volumes for 43 fields across 239 field-years; effective precipitation calculated as gridMET precipitation minus growing season deep percolation estimated from Deines et al. (2021) regressions.
(2) Water right group (WRG) scale: SD-6 LEMA subdivided into non-overlapping WRG combinations of pumping wells, fields, and authorized places of use; ET-based irrigation volumes compared against WIMAS metered withdrawals per WRG.
(3) Management area scale: total annual ET-based irrigation volumes compared against total metered withdrawals for all 203 irrigation wells within SD-6 LEMA boundary (2016-2020).
(4) Precipitation-adjusted bias correction: linear regression between irrigation volume residuals and precipitation used to improve ET-based calculations and identify conditions where ET-to-irrigation conversion systematically under- or over-estimates.
records.data_sources: OpenET ensemble mean (six RSET models, Google Earth Engine, monthly 2016-2022); gridMET 4km daily precipitation and ETo; USDA Cropland Data Layer (crop type); Annual Irrigation Maps (AIM, Deines et al. 2019, 30m Landsat binary irrigation presence); WIMAS metered pump records for 203 SD-6 wells; farmer-reported irrigation records for 43 voluntary fields.
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No formal crediting program evaluated. Study uses SD-6 LEMA as a validation test case because its mandatory metering infrastructure provides reliable ground truth for OpenET comparison. Findings are explicitly framed as informing whether satellite ET data can support water accounting and management policy at different scales.
records.key_finding: OpenET ensemble mean best agreement with metered irrigation occurs at growing-season timescale with mean absolute error of 81mm (bias 4.9%) at field scale and improves substantially at management area scale — but agreement degrades where deep percolation assumptions are violated, irrigation efficiency is low, or fields are partially irrigated, limiting direct applicability to fallowed or transitioning land without local calibration.
records.direct_quotes:
"We integrated ET data with several other geospatial datasets to calculate irrigation volumes and/or depths. We extracted OpenET data from Google Earth Engine at a monthly time step for 2016-2022... To estimate irrigation using our ET data, we calculated the precipitation deficit (ET - effective precipitation) for each field and masked it to only fields mapped as irrigated by AIM." (Methods, Section 2.2, p. 3)

"However, there were no eddy covariance towers near our study area... and therefore OpenET's accuracy for irrigated agriculture in semi-arid conditions typical of the western High Plains Aquifer has not been locally assessed." (Methods, Section 2.2, p. 4)
records.accounting_gap: ET-based irrigation calculations require locally calibrated deep percolation assumptions that are not available for most California GSAs. Performance degrades at field scale for partially irrigated fields, mixed-use parcels, and fields with high return flows. Negative precipitation deficits — which indicate non-irrigated or fallowed conditions — are masked to zero, meaning the approach cannot directly quantify ET changes for fallowed or transitioning land. No eddy covariance validation sites exist in the semi-arid western High Plains environment most analogous to the California Central Valley.
records.notes:
ET-minus-precipitation approach works well for active irrigated fields but not great at fallowed or transitioning land or partially irrigated fields.

The precipitation-adjusted bias correction method can be used to improve estimates for GSAs with good metered data.

Read alongside Deines et al. (2019) and Whittemore et al. (2023) as the third paper in the Kansas LEMA accounting trilogy.

records.citation: Zipper, S., Gambill, I., Schmitt, M., Kouba, C., Scantlebury, L., Harter, T., & Murphy, N.P. (2026). Lagged streamflow depletion due to pumping-induced stream drying: Incorporation into analytical streamflow depletion estimation methods. Journal of Hydrology, 667, 134909. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2026.134909
records.geography: Scott Valley (Scott River watershed), Siskiyou County, California, USA
records.accounting_method: Develops a water-budget-based method to incorporate pumping-induced stream drying and downstream depletion routing into Analytical Depletion Functions (ADFs). The stream network is represented as a directed graph; at each timestep, streamflow depletion is calculated only up to the amount of "water available" (i.e., estimated streamflow absent groundwater pumping) in a given segment; any depletion exceeding that amount is "banked" and applied to a later timestep once water becomes available again, propagating impacts from headwater to downstream segments. Results were validated against observed USGS gauge streamflow and against output from a process-based numerical model (SVIHM).
records.data_sources: USGS streamflow gauge data (Scott River at Fort Jones, gauge 11519500, records to 1941); Scott Valley Integrated Hydrologic Model (SVIHM) output (a MODFLOW-NWT-based process model); California Natural Flows Database (CNFD), a statewide statistical model of unimpaired monthly streamflow, tested as an alternative "water available" input for basins lacking a local numerical model
records.formal_program_or_crediting: No operational crediting or formal accounting program described; this is a methodological/decision-support tool. Authors frame the ADF-with-drying approach as "well-suited for integration into web-based decision support tools" for SGMA-related groundwater/surface water management, but do not describe an existing GSA program using it.
records.key_finding: ADFs incorporating stream drying closely matched observed Scott River streamflow (KGE = 0.91, R2 = 0.92, normalized RMSE = 5.9%) and SVIHM output, and accurately predicted how often streamflow dropped below management thresholds (MAE = 7.3%). The method resolves a core limitation of standard ADFs — the assumption of an infinite supply of water in the stream — by simulating stream drying and a resulting temporal lag: pumping-driven depletion during summer drying is "banked" and doesn't manifest as streamflow depletion until the stream network reconnects in fall/winter. This is directly relevant to GAP because it extends a low-cost, low-complexity accounting method (ADFs) so it can be applied credibly in non-perennial/intermittent stream settings — common across California — without requiring a full numerical groundwater model.
records.direct_quotes:
"ADFs incorporating stream drying have strong agreement with observed streamflow and SVIHM results" (Abstract).

"a substantial fraction of streamflow depletion is lagged until the stream network rewets in the fall/winter" (Abstract).

"ADFs using CNFD data simulate appropriate temporal dynamics but overestimate streamflow" (Abstract).

"This emerging ADF modeling framework is...well-suited for integration into web-based decision support tools" (Discussion, p. 13).
records.accounting_gap: Applying the CNFD (statewide unimpaired-flow) dataset as the "water available" input produced correct temporal dynamics but overestimated streamflow relative to the locally calibrated SVIHM, indicating regional statistical products alone are not yet accurate enough for basins without local bias-correction. The ADF-with-drying method also does not explicitly account for other pumping-related water balance changes (e.g., land-use conversion, changes in consumptive use/ET from irrigation) — the authors note it "could be enhanced by integration with...remotely sensed estimates of differences in consumptive water use" (Conclusions, p. 13). No uncertainty quantification for ADF estimates is yet built in, which the authors flag as necessary before decision-support integration.
records.notes:
Resolves a previously unaddressed methodological gap in intermittent/non-perennial stream accounting for streamflow depletion.
Demonstrates a path for extending low-cost ADF tools (vs. full numerical models like SVIHM) to ungauged/unmodeled basins using CNFD, which is significant for statewide GAP scalability. Developed by The Nature Conservancy and UC Davis researchers using a California SGMA basin (Scott Valley) as the test case.
